World.title: Hasan Piker is becoming the 'face of the progressive movement,' former Democratic operative warns
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Controversial Twitch streamer Hasan Piker has found himself at the center of a debate about the direction of the Democratic Party and generations of voters to come. However, recently on his stream, which he does for hours every day, the far-left commentator has claimed the media is making him out to have more influence than he actually does.

Evan Barker, author of "Nothing Left: Confessions Of A Democratic Operative," disagrees with Piker's analysis of his own popularity — he has more than 3 million followers on Twitch and millions more across other social media accounts — pointing to the increasing number of candidates who have invited him to campaign with them.

"Why would these candidates have this desire to bring him into their state, to campaign alongside him if he wasn't influential, to hold press junkets with him, to invite him to barbecues? Like, why would they be doing that if he didn't have influence? Like, clearly, he does," Barker told Fox News Digital.

Barker is no stranger to Democratic politics. She raised tens of millions of dollars for Democratic candidates, campaigned for Hillary Clinton and worked for candidates backed by Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y.

EX-DEM OPERATIVE DETAILS 'NEW DONOR ESTABLISHMENT' BEHIND MAMDANI-ERA PROGRESSIVES: 'NOT FROM THE GRASSROOTS'

Barker eventually broke with the party in 2024, a journey she details in her new book. She told Fox News Digital that Democrats are "testing their limits with the popularity" in areas of the country that aren't deep blue, especially when campaigning with Piker.

"It's one thing to appear on somebody's podcast, it's another to have them come campaign for you," she said.

Piker's hours-long stream primarily focuses on politics. He has backed several candidates in the 2026 cycle, including Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed and Wisconsin gubernatorial candidate Francesca Hong.

While El-Sayed won his primary race, Hong lost to Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, who has since said he was not planning on campaigning with Piker.

Piker's long history of incendiary and far-left rhetoric has made him an easy target for Republicans. From his retracted comments about saying the U.S. "deserved" 9/11, to his praise of Chinese dictator Mao Zedong, and the hours of talking he does every day, there's no shortage of comments for which Piker and his allies could be held to account.

When asked what she would tell candidates who are thinking about campaigning with the Twitch streamer, Barker told Fox News Digital that she would advise against it.

"I would say that the juice isn't worth the squeeze," she said. "Yeah, you're trying to appeal to younger voters, you're trying to drive out your base, but how do you win a general election aligning with him?"

DEMOCRAT ESTABLISHMENT STRIKES BACK AS SOCIALIST CANDIDATE DOWNED IN BATTLEGROUND PRIMARY

While Barker has expressed skepticism about Piker, she said she often hears those on the left defend their relationship with the streamer by comparing him to another media personality: Joe Rogan.

During the 2024 campaign cycle, then-Vice President Kamala Harris was criticized for not appearing on Rogan's widely followed podcast while running for president, particularly after both now-Vice President JD Vance and now-President Donald Trump sat for interviews with him. Some have made the case that Piker could serve as an alternative to Rogan, but Barker disagrees.

"Hasan Piker is not at all like Joe Rogan, actually. So, the charm of Joe Rogan, what makes his show so powerful, is that he talks about politics sometimes. Politics is sometimes peppered into his conversations, but by and large, the majority of the time, he's not talking about politics," she said. "Whereas Hasan Piker, that's pretty much all he talks about."

She also noted that some of Piker's rhetoric that appeals to younger voters might not resonate with larger populations in parts of the country that are not deep blue.

"At the end of the day, I would remind these progressive candidates, it's not just about pleasing your staff, it's not just about pleasing, you know, the young people that are in this movement. If you want to win places like Wisconsin, if you want to win places like Michigan, you have to be patriotic," she said. "The Rust Belt is filled with hardworking patriotic Americans who don't feel the way that Hasan Piker does."

WISCONSIN DEMOCRATIC VOTERS CHALK SOCIALIST FRANCESCA HONG'S STUNNING LOSS UP TO ELECTABILITY CONCERNS

As Democrats weigh the consequences of backlash for campaigning with Piker against the access to younger voters that he brings, Barker says the streamer is quickly becoming well known offline as well. She argued that Piker is "probably the biggest podcaster, live streamer" that the Democrats have at their disposal.

"He's quickly becoming a household name. He's quickly becoming the face of the progressive movement," she said.

Barker acknowledged that some progressives may not be "comfortable" with Piker as a de facto leader, calling his rise a "monster that they've created themselves." She also compared the current moment to previous shifts within the progressive movement, arguing that figures and ideas once embraced by the left are later dismissed as excesses of an earlier era.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

Barker pointed specifically to recent discussions of "Woke 1" after Ocasio-Cortez's invocation of the term last week, arguing that Democrats have yet to reckon with the consequences of that period around 2020, which was marked by a surge in racial identity politics and progressive groupthink.

"People's lives were ruined because of 'woke 1.' It wasn't just some mass delusion or mass hysteria that we all went through... It pushed people away from Democratic politics," she said.

Barker argued that Democrats' continued willingness to align with figures like Piker shows the party has yet to move beyond that period.

"I think that there needs to be a true reckoning in the progressive movement and in the Democratic Party for people to really be able to heal and move on from this," she said.

World.title: Surrogate gives birth in Texas to baby with heart defect after parents requested abortion
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A surrogate mother gave birth to a baby against its biological parents' wishes after fleeing to Texas with help from state Attorney General Ken Paxton.

Surrogate mother McKenna West fled to Texas after her baby was diagnosed with hypoplastic left heart syndrome around the time West was 20 weeks pregnant. The diagnosis allegedly prompted the baby's birth parents to ask West to have an abortion, Paxton's office wrote in a news release Tuesday.

After West went to Texas, Paxton intervened, formally notifying UT Southwestern Medical Center and Children’s Medical Center of Dallas of their legal obligations to provide the baby with "medically necessary, life-saving care upon birth," his office wrote.

DEM GOV MAURA HEALEY SIGNS SWEEPING MASSACHUSETTS BILL ALLOWING ABORTIONS UP TO BIRTH

"The court has made the right decision in immediately acting to protect baby Gabriel’s life and ensure he receives the care he deserves," Paxton said in the statement.

"My office utilized every tool at our disposal to protect life, and we will not back down in continuing to support baby Gabriel’s well-being. Every child in our state deserves to be cared for and protected, and that’s exactly what I’ll fight for."

"While the surrogate mother of baby Gabriel has traveled to Texas for protection and care for Gabriel, the intended parents have refused to agree that they will consent to the life-saving surgery for Gabriel after he is born. Attorney General Paxton has now secured a legal victory that will ensure baby Gabriel’s life is protected and that care is provided," Paxton's office added.

West's baby, named Gabriel, was born Wednesday, according to Fox News' Kerri Urbahn. Gabriel was brought to a neonatal intensive care unit, where doctors could soon perform lifesaving surgery.

SUPREME COURT UNANIMOUSLY SLAPS DOWN BLUE STATE TARGETING PRO-LIFE GROUP

The hospital where the surgery would likely be performed has a 100% success rate on the procedure, Urbahn reported.

"Baby Gabriel deserves a chance at life, and I will not allow anyone to unlawfully deny him medically necessary care," Paxton said. "My office will use every tool available to protect innocent lives and ensure that every child receives the care required under Texas law."

World.title: Socialist insurgency heads to Trump’s backyard, targets pro-Israel Democrat
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

The high-stakes battle for the ideological future of the Democratic Party moves to Florida next week, before heading to New England early next month, as the 2026 primary season wraps up.

After impactful left-wing victories this month by Michigan's Abdul El-Sayed and Minnesota Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan in crucial Democratic Senate primaries, and a searing setback for the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), with the downing of DSA member Francesca Hong in Wisconsin's Democratic gubernatorial primary, the next faceoff in the party's civil war comes Tuesday in Florida.

That's where DSA endorsed Oliver Larkin is challenging more moderate Democratic Rep. Jared Moskowitz in a key congressional swing district that's among roughly two dozen House seats that will determine if Republicans hold onto their razor-thin majority in the midterm elections.

DEMOCRATIC GROUP LAUNCHES $15 MILLION WAR ON DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS: 'MORTAL DANGER'

Two weeks later, the party's divisions return to a statewide stage, as longtime progressive leader Sen. Ed Markey of Massachusetts is facing a serious primary challenge from more moderate Democratic Rep. Seth Moulton.

A left-versus-center battle is brewing a week later in neighboring New Hampshire, in the party's Senate primary for a crucial battleground seat Democrats must hold in the midterm elections in order to win back the chamber's majority from the GOP.

Progressives scored their biggest victory to date a week ago, when El-Sayed narrowly edged moderate Rep. Haley Stevens to capture the party's Senate nomination in the Great Lakes battleground, in the race to succeed retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters.

DEMOCRATIC GROUP LAUNCHES $15 MILLION WAR ON DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS: 'MORTAL DANGER'

On Tuesday, Flanagan downed moderate Democratic Rep. Angie Craig by roughly 20 points, to grab the party's nomination in blue-leaning but competitive Minnesota, in the race to succeed another retiring Democrat, Sen. Tina Smith.

Both El-Sayed and Flanagan were backed by top far-left leaders, including progressive champion Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont.

But in Wisconsin's Democratic gubernatorial showdown, Hong was upset by a razor-thin margin by Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, who was backed by retiring Democratic Gov. Tony Evers.

Evers and Crowley, pointing to Hong's past controversial comments on defunding the police and criticizing Thanksgiving, argued that a Hong primary victory would have boosted GOP nominee Rep. Tom Tiffany's chances of flipping the Wisconsin governor's mansion.

With the primary calendar winding down, here's a closer look at the final nomination faceoffs that are dividing Democrats and giving Republicans plenty of ammunition to use in the midterms.

Florida

The 33-year-old Larkin, a veteran of Sanders' 2016 Democratic presidential campaign, is also the only DSA-endorsed House candidate running in a crucial congressional swing district.

Larkin says he supports abolishing the U.S. Senate, arguing in a Fox News interview that it's an "undemocratic institution."

He agreed with socialist New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu should have been arrested during his recent trip to the U.S., and refers to Israel's ruling coalition as a "religious supremacist regime."

Moskowitz is a strong and vocal supporter of Israel, who has advocated for robust U.S. military and security assistance.

DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB

The two-term federal lawmaker and former state representative and Florida FEMA director is running for re-election in the state's newly redrawn 25th Congressional District, a Broward County-anchored seat in the southeastern corner of the red-leaning state.

Moskowitz, who enjoys establishment backing from the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, is also supported by AIPAC, a major-Israel aligned political group. Larkin enjoys plenty of support from top far-left leaders, including controversial political streamer Hasan Piker. Moskowitz is the polling and fundraising lead over Larkin heading into the primary.

Massachusetts

Markey is backed by a slew of progressive politicians and groups, including Sanders and Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts, as well as fellow Bay Stater Rep. Ayanna Pressley, a member of the far-left Squad.

SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

Moulton is supported by a smaller group of more moderate Democratic lawmakers and groups.

While the primary is partially viewed as a progressive versus moderate showdown, the Democratic Party's generational showdown is very much at play in this contest.

The 80-year-old Markey has served in Congress for half a century, first in the House and since 2013 in the Senate. The 47-year-old Moulton has repeatedly emphasized it's time for a new generation of leaders.

The push by Democrats for generational change was fueled two years ago by then-81-year-old President Joe Biden's exit from the presidential race amid questions over his physical and mental stamina following a disastrous debate performance against President Donald Trump.

A similar generational fight is being waged in the Democratic primary in Massachusetts' 8th Congressional District. That's where 71-year-old Rep. Stephen Lynch, who has served in the House for a quarter-century, is being primary challenged by 39-year-old Patrick Roath.

New Hampshire

The action moves north a week later to neighboring New Hampshire, where longtime Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, the first woman in the nation's history elected governor and to the Senate, is retiring.

Four-term Rep. Chris Pappas is the front-runner for the Democratic nomination, and enjoys plenty of establishment backing, including from Shaheen and the Granite State's other Democrat in the chamber, Sen. Maggie Hassan.

Pappas is the clear polling and fundraising leader in a race that also includes medical scientist Karishma Manzur, who is backed by a handful of progressive groups.

A backer of Israel, Pappas has been blasted over the support he's receiving from AIPAC by Manzur, who argues Israeli has committed "genocide" against Palestinians in its war with Hamas in Gaza.

Fox News' Matthew Donnell contributed to this report.

A luxury $9.1 million yacht sank into the waters of the Mediterranean Sea Tuesday, just days after it had been delivered to its new owner.

The Angiola II was off the coast of Porto Cervo on the popular Italian island of Sardinia with 14 guests on board when it experienced engine failure that sparked a fire, the New York Post reported.

The blaze damaged seals on the vessel, which began to take on water, causing it to tip onto its side.

DRUNK REPEAT OFFENDER CALLED A 'TICKING TIME BOMB' BEFORE 80-MPH BOATING COLLISION KILLED WOMAN: PROSECUTORS

Video footage showed the boat on its side.

COAST GUARD OPENS FIRE ON BOAT SMUGGLING 25 CHINESE NATIONALS NEAR FLORIDA AFTER IT REFUSED TO STOP

The unidentified owner — an Italian businessman — was the last one off the ship, the newspaper reported.

The yacht reportedly sank at a depth of around 23 feet between an island called L’Isola dei Cappuccini and Capo Ferro on Sardinia’s exclusive Costa Smeralda, or Emerald Coast, the news report states.

The boat will be kept under surveillance until a recovery company recovers it from the sea floor.

World.title: Baseball fans fume at MLB's 'Field of Dreams' game decision, reporter Tricia Whitaker has a boat day & LLWS!
World.content:
'Nightcaps' is a daily column that catches you up on the biggest sports, news and culture stories you may have missed while pretending to do work at your desk. It runs Monday–Friday on OutKick.com.

Over the hump and safely into a big Thursday filled with actual NFL football (kind of) and an MLB Field of Dreams game only the 1%ers can watch.

What a blessing. What a day! Are things starting to ramp up, or what? And who knows! Maybe by the end of this class, the WNBA will have figured out what a woman is.

HOME RUN DERBY RATINGS CRASH ON NETFLIX, SETS 20-PLUS-YEAR LOW AS QUESTIONS SURFACE ABOUT PROGRAM QUALITY

I wouldn't hold your breath, but there's always a chance.

Welcome to a Thursday Nightcaps — the one where Pat Sajak, of all people, points out the lunacy in tonight's annual Field of Dreams game.

Pat Sajak! We usually only check in with Maggie Sajak in this class. I believe Pat's a first-timer. Welcome aboard!

What else? I've got a couple wild moments yesterday in the world of little league baseball, Apple TV's Tricia Whitaker enjoyed a Canadian cottage getaway and Lordy, did you guys have some steak takes on the heels of yesterday's class.

Well done. We'll dive in.

Take out a second mortgage, grab you a Netflix subscription and settle in for a Thursday 'Cap!

Pat Sajak isn't a fan of the Netflix Field of Dreams game

I think Major League Baseball does a lot of things right. Frankly, they're probably the best sport when it comes to doing things that make sense.

Look at the mess that is the WNBA right now and compare it to MLB. It's laughable.

The pitch clock was brilliant. I've come around on the ghost runner. ABS has very clearly worked. The Home Run Derby and the All-Star game are the two best exhibition events in sports (not a high bar, to be fair).

The Field of Dreams game has been a home run since its debut way back in 2021. It's perfect. Everything about it is perfect.

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

This year — tonight — is the first year it won't be on Fox. Instead, it was scooped up by Netflix during last year's TV negotiations.

Yes, that means if you really want to watch some Phillies-Twins action tonight from Iowa, you're gonna have to pay up.

And when folks realize this... look out.

In fact, one already has:

What a night for the little leaguers!

Does it seem a bit ironic that MLB’s Field of Dreams game — which harkens back to a simpler, more bucolic time — is being streamed on Netflix?

You know what, Pat Sajak? You are 1000% right. What a rip-off! More importantly, what a vocabulary on 79-year-old Pat Sajak! Bucolic? I'm not sure I've ever seen that word in my life. Does Pat still have the fastball, or what?

Bucolic, by the way, is an adjective that means relating to the pleasant, peaceful aspects of the countryside, country life, or shepherds, according to the stupid AI bot that runs Google now.

Pat wasn't alone in his bewilderment, by the way:

I could go on and on. Nobody is happy. Is anyone ever happy?

For those still on the fence, a Netflix subscription costs $8.99 a month (with ads). If you really hate ads, you have to pony up a whopping $20 a month. And if you really hate ads AND regular 1080p HD, you have to pay $27 for the 4K version.

Thank God I'm a T-Mobile customer. Free MLB TV and Netflix included! What a deal.

(Not a promotion, but I wouldn't mind if it was.)

OK, let's keep this class moving ... from the big diamond to the little diamond! What a night we had in the Little League World Series regionals last night.

We had:

A coach give a pitcher a sermon on the mound.

A coach get tossed.

And, a player leap over the catcher at home plate.

What a sport:

Tricia and STEAK!

Thoughts? First impressions?

The coach who gave a sermon on the mound (come on, that's a good one!) is taking a little heat today because folks say he should've been out there giving a scouting report instead. Boots on the ground say the next three batters reached safely, and Arizona went on to lose.

Not great! For what it's worth, my little league coach used to tell me, "Zach, if you strike out, there are a billion people in China who will wake up tomorrow and won't care."

Decent advise for a 12-year-old, I reckon. But we also never got anywhere close to Williamsport, so perhaps we could've used some more motivation.

As for the coach who got tossed ... that's nothing. I grew up with a coach who used to get thrown out every week for arguing anything and everything under the sun. During one All-Star game in particular, he snuck back into the complex Bobby Valentine style and hung out behind the outfield fence.

That's called commitment. Loved Coach Tony.

OK, let's rapid-fire this Thursday class into a big Thursday night of preseason football. First up? Yesterday, I gave you my Mount Rushmore of Steaks to celebrate National Filet Mignon Day.

From Larry K in Iowa:

Anything that moos is my favorite meat. I grew up a meat and potatoes kid. Still am 7 decades later. Ribeyes and Kansas City strips are my favorites. My smoker will be fired up this weekend.

Thanks, Larry! Bring a couple over to the Field of Dreams game!

From Tom J. in Omaha:

I have two:

Ribeye on the bone — the bone must be there with no questions asked – it’s not the same eating a boneless ribeye.

Porterhouse — which you cannot go wrong, and it is of course two steaks in one on a big bone — so technically, number 2 and 3 would equal a porterhouse.

Thanks, Tom! Agree wholeheartedly on the bone-in Ribeye. Huge difference.

And, From Ryan N:

Agree with your steak rankings. Up until end of last year I never even considered ordering anything but a ribeye, but I’ve been on a filet tear so far this year. For me it’s more about portion control than anything else. I can’t be knocking down 14+ oz ribeyes all the time anymore.

It's football season, Ryan. Portion control, shmortion control! Let's get the ribeyes back in the rotation and worry about the waistline in January.

OK, that's it for today. Good work, everyone. Six NFL preseason games tonight and the Field of Dreams game for those who have a rich uncle who recently kicked the bucket.

Here's Apple TV's MLB girl, Tricia Whitaker, to get everyone ready.

See you tomorrow.

World.title: Kennedy Center board votes to partially close arts center during renovations and add Trump’s name to the building again
World.content:
The Trump-appointed Kennedy Center board on Thursday voted to partially close the iconic arts center for up to two years during renovations and to re-add President Donald Trump’s name to the building’s facade, according to one person who attended the virtual board meeting and a second person familiar with the meeting.

The decision would close the Kennedy Center’s main building while keeping a smaller addition, known as the Reach, open for some events in response to a May court order requiring the board to maintain the center as a memorial to President John F. Kennedy.

After an almost two-hour Zoom meeting, the board voted 20 to 3 to change the name of the building to “The John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts Restored and Renovated by President Donald J. Trump” and the physical location to “President Donald J. Trump Plaza.” Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick proposed the name change.

Trump, who appointed himself chairman of the board last year, joined the call for several minutes, according to the source who attended the meeting.

The three people voting against it were the ex officio members from Congress, Rep. Joyce Beatty, D-Ohio, Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I., and Rep. Rick Larsen, D-Wash.

“This latest development is a transparent effort to circumvent the Court’s ruling, and flies in the face of the statutes that Congress passed,” Beatty, who was one of the plaintiffs in a lawsuit challenging the Kennedy Center’s renaming, said in a statement. “I will continue to fight for this treasured national monument.”

Attorneys for Beatty said in a statement the new naming effort appears to defy a judge’s ruling earlier this year that the center’s board does not have the authority to rename what was intended as a “living memorial” for an assassinated president.

“A federal judge already rejected the board’s unlawful attempt to rename the Kennedy Center, and told Donald Trump’s handpicked board that its last closure vote was ill-informed and preordained. Today’s vote is more of the same, and a show of blatant disrespect to the courts,” said the lawyers, Norm Eisen of Democracy Defenders Action and Nathaniel Zelinsky of Washington Litigation Group.

U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper’s May order, which temporarily blocked the Kennedy Center’s planned closure last month, also asked that the board provide a financial plan to justify the decision to close the center. Keeping the smaller venue open would allow ticket sales for some events, including performances by the National Symphony Orchestra, which is the chief tenant of the Kennedy Center.

The orchestra has performed there since the early 1970s when the Center — conceived by Jaqueline Kennedy as a memorial to her slain husband — first opened.

In recent years, under the baton of Music Director and Principal Conductor Giancarlo Noseda, it has been rising in stature — but its future is now uncertain because the Kennedy Center’s Concert Hall will not be available. A search for other venues in the area has been underway.

The Kennedy Center’s future has been in limbo for months as Trump moves to reshape the iconic art institution in his image, one of several major Washington, D.C., renovation projects.

After Trump named himself the Kennedy Center’s chairman last year and filled its board with allies, the board in March voted unanimously to close the center for two years for renovations.

Cooper’s order temporarily blocked the construction work and ordered that the president’s name be removed from the building, which it was in June.

He also said that the board could still ultimately close the center “should it come to this decision anew after independently balancing its multiple obligations to the Center in a prudent fashion.”

The judge also found the board did not have the authority to rename the center or add a name to it without the approval of Congress, which initially named it.

“The Kennedy Center’s organic statute makes crystal clear that the Center is to be named for President Kennedy, and it cannot bear any other formal name or public memorial based on the Board’s unilateral say-so,” Cooper said in his May decision.

“May the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts be renamed absent Congressional authorization? The answer, plain from the face of the statute, is no. Nor can any other individual be memorialized on the front portico of the building. Congress gave the Kennedy Center its name, and only Congress can change it.”

The decision to close the center and add Trump’s name to the building has sparked outrage from the administration’s critics, as well as members of the Kennedy family.

Former Rep. Joseph Kennedy III, a grandnephew of the late president, said in a statement last year that the center “is a living memorial to a fallen president and named for President Kennedy by federal law. It can no sooner be renamed than can someone rename the Lincoln Memorial, no matter what anyone says.”

World.title: Ticks that cause Lyme and other diseases have migrated south. Are doctors ready?
World.content:
Angela Newman of Biltmore Forest, North Carolina, remembers the “bizarre” symptoms she began experiencing almost a decade ago. Blurry vision, a stiff neck, hypersensitive skin, numbness and weakness that would come and go.

She saw a variety of medical specialists, undergoing an MRI, CT scan and psychiatric assessments. The doctors often dismissed her symptoms as anxiety or depression, Newman, 57, said.

Angela Newman hiking the Appalachian Trail near her home in North Carolina. Her experience with Lyme disease prompted research into the migration of ticks southward. Angela Newman

Finally, at a college reunion she mentioned her illness to a friend who recognized the mysterious symptoms as a possible case of Lyme disease.

When she called her primary doctor for a Lyme disease test, he told her, “I don’t think you have Lyme. We don’t really have that around here,” Newman said. “I said ‘I don’t care what you think. I want you to test me.’”

The results were positive, a diagnosis that took five years to make. Within days of receiving antibiotics, her symptoms started to abate. It took nearly a year to feel like her usual, energetic self.

“I knew I wasn’t crazy,” she said. “It’s frustrating to have people basically say, ‘I think you need antidepressants.’”

Newman never found a tick but had noticed a welt on her leg that looked a little bit like a spider bite.

At the time Newman was infected in North Carolina with Lyme, the disease was believed to be largely limited to the Northeast. New research published Thursday by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention underscores how the bugs have gained a foothold in unexpected places farther south.

“It was always thought that Rocky Mountain spotted fever, which is caused by different bacteria, was our major tick-borne disease,” said University of North Carolina School of Medicine’s Dr. Ross Boyce, the CDC study’s author and a researcher who specializes in tick-borne diseases.

The new research “is the slam dunk,” he said, proving that Lyme disease should be considered a major threat to areas farther south than previously thought.

World.title: Surveillance company Flock moves to increase oversight after police misuse
World.content:
Flock Safety, the police tech company that tracks Americans’ vehicle movements through a line of cameras, announced Thursday that it would implement several new safeguards to its products.

The changes that Flock outlined include shrinking the period for how long it holds people’s movement data by default, going from one month to one week, the company said in a news release. In cases where an officer wants to hold data longer, they will be prompted to enter a case number.

To address potential police abuse of Flock’s data on people, the company also plans to fully deploy a system it began testing earlier this year, called Audit Assistance, that will lock out a user whose searches display “abnormal activity,” the release said.

A spokesperson told NBC News that the changes are meant to help address privacy concerns and to stem officer abuse of the cameras, which have prompted some cities to cancel their Flock contracts amid a national wave of vandalism against them. But the American Civil Liberties Union, a long-standing Flock critic, downplayed the new changes as minor.

“My biggest concern was and will continue to be that they are a mass surveillance company that collects billions and billions of license plate scans every month on people who have done nothing wrong,” said Chad Marlow, senior policy counsel at the ACLU.

Flock makes a range of high-tech surveillance products but is best known for its nationwide fleet of automated license plate readers, pole-mounted cameras that log cars as they pass popular roads and intersections, creating a massive database of each car’s movement, license plate number, make and model, and time of travel.

While the system has been championed by many police forces, privacy concerns have grown. Law enforcement offices that contract with Flock do not need a warrant to access travel information and can opt to share their data with local law enforcement offices, statewide or nationwide, creating a database of Americans’ real-time movements accessible to a range of police officers that spans much of the country.

Flock and law enforcement officers who rely on the technology say that it can be an invaluable tool for tracking suspects and can save policing hours. But privacy advocates say that the cameras sweep up unwitting Americans into a giant dragnet, and police officers have been repeatedly accused of stalking people with the technology.

Marlow said that while he welcomed Flock’s shortening its default data retention time (a week is still short of the ACLU’s recommended 48 hours), the company’s proposed reforms did little to address his concerns with license plate tracking.

“Flock collects location data on virtually every car in America every month and then facilitates the nationwide sharing of that data where it can be used to target members of vulnerable and disfavored communities and to undermine the privacy and chill the behavior of everyone in America,” Marlow said.

World.title: Haitians in Ohio who lost protected status get ankle monitors instead of ICE detention
World.content:
Haitians living in Ohio who’ve lost their protected status are increasingly getting ankle monitors instead of being detained by immigration officers, attorneys say.

ICE has been alerting Haitians to appear in person at check-ins, where they are given ankle monitors to track their whereabouts until an immigration judge can decide whether they may have a legitimate reason to remain in the country, such as an asylum claim, according to the lawyers.

The decision is often made over a lack of detention space for more than 300,000 Haitians who lost Temporary Protected Status after a Supreme Court decision in June, a senior Department of Homeland Security official said.

“We were really worried that this was going to be a mass enforcement, mass detention operation,” said Katie Kersh, an immigration attorney who represents Haitian clients as part of her work at the Ohio-based law firm Advocates for Basic Legal Equality.

Instead, Kersh said, several of her clients recently received ICE letters mandating the in-person check-ins. “And so we went,” she said. People were arrested but not detained for the long term. “They all have these ankle monitors and they’re not allowed to travel outside of a 75-mile radius from their home.”

DHS declined to comment on the ankle monitors. “DHS does not discuss ongoing or future operations,” a spokesperson said in an emailed statement.

“What we would say now is it’s closing time, which means you don’t have to go home, but you can’t stay here.”

It is the latest policy shift since DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin took over in March that could draw President Donald Trump’s ire. Last month, Mullin ran afoul of President Donald Trump when he announced a halt on vehicle pursuits by ICE after fatal shootings.

The ankle monitors and other trackers allow immigrants to continue to live in the U.S. while their cases play out. The program was bolstered under the Biden administration but Trump’s immigration policy architect, Stephen Miller, prefers holding immigrants in detention.

A senior administration official and DHS official told NBC News recently there was growing tension between the White House and Mullin, this administration’s second Homeland Security secretary, though the president does not appear to be preparing to oust him.

Temporary Protected Status is a humanitarian program created by Congress that allows people from countries ravaged by war, natural disasters or other extreme circumstances to come and live and work in the United States temporarily.

In June, the Supreme Court allowed the Trump administration to end the protections for more than 300,000 Haitians who came to the country following the 2010 earthquake, and the more than 50,000 Syrians who came when the civil war broke out in their country in 2015. Previous administrations and lower courts had determined the conditions in both of those countries were still too dire to end protections against deportations there.

The order has sowed confusion among business owners who employ Haitians, and employees who have been unsure when or how they should show up to work.

The senior DHS official said it would be impossible to hold the more than 300,000 Haitians in the U.S. who lost their protected status in ICE detention. ICE currently is holding about 65,000 immigrants in detention facilities across the country, until a judge can hear their case. NBC has reported ICE is working to open new detention facilities.

Last month, Mullin instructed ICE officers to pause vehicle stops following two fatal shootings of men in vehicles, but the policy was quickly overturned by Trump. Mullin had not run the pause by the White House, NBC News reported, citing a senior administration official.

Trump has repeatedly focused on Haitian immigrants in the United States.

On the campaign trail in 2024, Trump and his running mate, Vice President JD Vance lent credence to false rumors that began on social media that a Haitian immigrant in Springfield, Ohio, had eaten a cat.

“In Springfield, the people that came in, they’re eating the dogs … they’re eating the cats,” Trump said in a September 2024 debate with then-Vice President Kamala Harris.

The Facebook post that sparked the rumor was later debunked, but Trump’s rhetoric fired up immigration hard-liners who supported him in the election.

World.title: The showdowns and reunions highlighting the NBA’s 2026-27 season
World.content:
The NBA’s offseason was defined by team-switching superstars — which meant that when the league released its schedule Thursday, its regular-season schedule was highlighted by those stars’ returns to the cities that once cheered for them.

During the 2026-27 season, Giannis Antetokounmpo will return to Milwaukee following a yearslong drama concerning whether he wanted to stay or leave. Jaylen Brown will play in Boston less than three years removed from bringing the Celtics an NBA championship. And Brown’s new Philadelphia teammate, LeBron James, will revisit Los Angeles after eight years as a Laker.

Whether they will be received warmly or not won’t be known until tipoff. But fans already know now when matchups like that, and other highly anticipated games, will be played.

Brown vs. Tatum in Boston

Only two years after winning NBA Finals MVP for Boston, Brown was traded by the Celtics to division rival Philadelphia in a move interpreted as the Celtics choosing Brown’s former running mate, Jayson Tatum, over him. Brown later said he “threw my phone across the room” after hearing of being dealt. Rather than hold the juicy reunion early in the season, the league dated his Boston return for Jan. 21. (On Prime Video) That game is one of four between the 76ers and Celtics this season, including Nov. 10 (Prime Video), Feb. 7 (NBC/Peacock) and March 7 (ABC).

Giannis returns to Milwaukee

Antetokounmpo’s breakup with Milwaukee, the team that drafted him and where he won a championship in 2021, was long. The NBA didn’t rush his return to Milwaukee, either. Antetokounmpo’s Miami Heat first visit the Bucks on Jan. 28, near the midway point of the season when it will be easier to gauge how successful his departure for Miami has gone. (On Prime Video)

Lillard’s Portland homecoming

After spending the first 11 years of his career adored in Portland, guard Damian Lillard left the city in a cantankerous exit in 2023 for Milwaukee to give Antetokounmpo what was supposed to be a championship boost. That partnership never lived up to such expectations, however, and Lillard re-signed with Portland last season but never played a game while rehabbing a long-term leg injury. That changes this season. If Lillard is healthy to begin the season as expected, the first home game of his second Portland chapter will take place Oct. 21 against Phoenix.

LeBron returns to L.A.

The Christmas Day slate includes LeBron James in his first game facing the Lakers in Los Angeles since deciding to become a free agent and joining Philadelphia. (On ABC/ESPN)

Trae Young’s first game in Atlanta

Once an All-Star whom the Atlanta Hawks oriented their franchise around, guard Trae Young was traded unceremoniously to Washington last season and played only five games with the Wizards before signing a long-term extension with the team this offseason. None of those games in a Wizards uniform came against his former team, though. Young will first play in Atlanta on Nov. 6.

How will Memphis welcome Morant?

Similar to Young in Atlanta, Ja Morant was once an untouchable trade asset when he launched to superstardom to begin his career in Memphis. Injuries and off-court discipline led the team to unload him this offseason to Portland. Morant will first play in Memphis on Feb. 6 (Prime Video).

A Knicks villain returns to New York

With big shots and brash confidence, Tyrese Haliburton became the player Knicks fans loved to hate while leading Indiana past New York and into the 2025 NBA Finals. After spending all of last season recovering from an Achilles’ tendon tear suffered in the Finals, Haliburton is set to return to Madison Square Garden against the reigning-champion Knicks on Nov. 22. Expect boos.

Three meetings between West finalists

The Western Conference’s path to the Finals last season was decided by a seven-game series between Oklahoma City and San Antonio, a pair of young rivals that could determine the conference’s fate for years to come, too. This season they will meet three times during the regular season in games that will instantly become circled on many fans’ calendars: Oct. 20 (NBC/Peacock), Feb. 11 (Prime Video) and March 14 (ABC).

Four games between perennial playoff foes

It wouldn’t be considered a historic rivalry, but Denver and Minnesota has become one of the best active matchups in the league after meeting in the first round three times in the last four years. They will play four times in the regular season, on Dec. 28 (NBC/Peacock), Dec. 31 (Prime Video), Jan. 27 (ESPN) and March 7 (ABC).

The ‘what-if?’ games

Few would have considered LeBron James a potential teammate of Stephen Curry when they faced one another during four consecutive NBA Finals from 2015-18. The two nearly joined forces this summer in Golden State, however, when James became a free agent and had the opportunity to ride out some of the last years of the aging superstars’ careers together. Instead, they continue to be on opposite sidelines, with Curry’s Warriors facing James and the 76ers twice, on March 24 and March 31.

No. 1 pick vs. No. 2

It’s not just the established superstars that fans will want to watch. The first two picks in the most recent draft, Washington’s AJ Dybantsa and Utah’s Darryn Peterson, will first play Feb. 27.

Led by Wembanyama, the NBA takes Europe

As the NBA continues to build out its plan to operate a league in Europe perhaps as soon as next year, it will take two regular-season games there. San Antonio’s French-born star Victor Wembanyama will be showcased when the Spurs play New Orleans in Paris on Jan. 14, and again Jan. 17 in Manchester, England. The latter game will mark the first time a regular-season game has been held in Manchester, in perhaps a test run for a market that is among the targets to potentially host an NBA Europe franchise. (Both on Prime Video)

World.title: Kennedy Center board votes to restore Trump's name on building
World.content:
The Kennedy Center's board of trustees voted Thursday to add President Trump's name to the facade of the performing arts center, more than two months after a judge ordered its removal, according to a House Democrat who sits on the center's board.

The board — which Mr. Trump filled with his allies — chose to add the phrase "Restored and Renovated By President Donald J. Trump" to the end of the center's formal name, the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, Democratic Rep. Joyce Beatty of Ohio and her lawyers said in a statement. Beatty said the board also voted to close the center for two years.

The vote marks a second attempt to put the president's name on the outside of the building, after U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper ruled in May that a decision to rename the center after both Kennedy and Mr. Trump violated the federal law that created the organization. Cooper also blocked the center from moving forward with a plan to close until 2028 for renovations, though the cultural institution had said it was still considering a partial or full closure.

Cooper issued his order in response to a lawsuit from Beatty. On Thursday, the congresswoman called the latest move "a transparent effort to circumvent the Court's ruling, and flies in the face of the statutes that Congress passed."

"Today's vote is more of the same, and a show of blatant disrespect to the courts," two of Beatty's attorneys, Norm Eisen and Nathaniel Zelinsky, wrote in the statement. "The court already ruled against the board when it bowed to Trump's demands. Now, the defendants must answer for their actions—again—in court."

White House spokesperson Liz Huston said: "Under President Trump's bold leadership, the Kennedy Center is on its way to becoming the finest cultural institution anywhere in the world."

CBS News has reached out to the Kennedy Center for comment.

Since returning to office last year, the president has sought to put his stamp on the Kennedy Center, replacing board members with longtime supporters who elected him chair of the organization. The changes to the center have drawn backlash from performers and congressional Democrats, leading some artists to cancel their appearances.

Then, late last year, the board voted to rename the organization as "The John F. Kennedy and The Donald J. Trump Memorial Center for the Performing Arts," which the center framed as a way of recognizing Mr. Trump's efforts to revamp the center. The president's name was then placed above Kennedy's name on the building's stone facade.

The board also voted in March to shut down for two years, arguing the building was in need of sweeping renovations.

Beatty sued over the changes, arguing the board doesn't have the authority to temporarily shutter the Kennedy Center or change its name without permission from Congress. Her lawyers noted that the center's name — and its role as a memorial to Kennedy — are enshrined in federal law, and the board is legally required to ensure that "no additional memorials or plaques" are installed on the site.

Cooper, an Obama-appointed judge, sided with Beatty in late May, ruling: "Congress gave the Kennedy Center its name, and only Congress can change it." He also said the decision to shut down all operations during the center's renovations was based on "an insufficient, one-sided presentation of information," and the board "neglected to consider the full range of its statutory obligations and potential adverse consequences of closure."

The metallic letters that spelled out Mr. Trump's name were then removed from the building overnight on June 13, after an appeals court declined to step in at the last minute and allow the name to stay up. Two months later, the scaffolding and tarp that were placed in front of the building to remove the lettering are still up.

Mr. Trump responded to Cooper's ruling by sharply criticizing the judge — arguing he should be impeached — and vowing to cut off his involvement with the Kennedy Center.

"So now, the Kennedy Center will collapse, both structurally and financially," the president wrote on Truth Social in May.

World.title: State Police investigators testify about search history in Lindsay Clancy trial
World.content:
Lindsay Clancy's trial for the murders of her three children in Massachusetts resumed Thursday with a 13th day of testimony as State Police investigators took the stand.

Massachusetts State Police Sgt. Kyle Pavao, who once worked in the cybercrime unit, was the first prosecution witness on the stand. His testimony began around 9:45 a.m. He examined the Microsoft Surface Pro taken from Clancy's home in early 2023.

Massachusetts State Police Trooper Kyle Pavao testifies in the murder trial of Lindsay Clancy on Aug. 13, 2026, in Plymouth, Mass. Josh Reynolds /AP Photo/Pool

He was asked, "Did your initial review of the extraction show a visit to a website entitled 'suicide methods' on Aug. 23, 2022?" "It did," Pavao replied.

Pavao also testified that the site mentioning suicide was accessed through a series of clicks on the Wikipedia page for singer-songwriter Tom Hall, who died by suicide. Pavao said that someone had searched for Tom Hall on Google after listening to him on Spotify.

The prosecution concluded its questioning and Lindsay Clancy's attorney, Kevin Reddington, began his cross-examination just after 10 a.m.

Reddington questioned Pavao about whether or not someone else could've been logged in to Clancy's account on the computer and said that Clancy's husband at the time, Patrick Clancy, "loved Tom Hall."

"That search was not actually methods of suicide; it was from the Tom Hall link," Reddington said. "You don't know if it was Lindsay Clancy who used the computer to search Tom Hall."

Pavao wrapped up his time on the stand just before 10:30 a.m. after a redirect and recross-examination.

Lindsay Clancy's notes, texts

Timothy Chiappini, a former State Police detective for Plymouth County, took the stand after Pavao. He currently works as a unit commander for the State Police critical investigations team. He testified that he was asked to do a forensic analysis of Clancy's iPhone.

Lindsay Clancy in Plymouth Superior Court on Aug. 13, 2026, in Plymouth, Mass. AP Photo/Josh Reynolds/Pool

Chiappini read entries from Clancy's notes app on Oct. 25, 2022.

"I am sad and depressed because I cannot parent my third child like my first. I want to treat every one of my babies like my first. But I know that's not a feasible possibility. I am sad I stopped breastfeeding. I feel not as connected with Cal now. I think I sort of I resent my other children because they prevent me from treating Cal like my first baby. And I know that's not fair to them. I know that. I was feeling so depressed last evening when Cora and Dawson came home from school. I know it runs off on them so we had a pretty rough evening. I want to feel love and connection with all my kids. I'm also probably having a bit of an internal conflict because my whole life I've wanted to have a lot of kids. I still don't want Cal to be our last, but I have a lot of figuring out to do before I have another. I'm on the fence about starting a new medication for anxiety/depression. I just want to feel happy. I want to be able to relax and take care of my kids. And when they go to bed at night, I want to deeply relax and hang out with Pat and then fall into a deep sleep for 8 hours, get up and pour hard into myself for an hour and a half. Cal was so very planned and desired. I want to be able to give him all the love he deserves," Chiappini read in court.

The prosecution also asked Chiappini about text messages and calls from Clancy's phone between her and Patrick on Jan. 24, 2023, the day Lindsay Clancy killed her three young children. Chiappini read out several messages between the two where Patrick and Clancy discussed getting takeout for dinner at a restaurant called ThreeV.

Timothy Chiappini testifies during the murder trial of Lindsay Clancy on Aug. 13, 2026, in Plymouth, Mass. Josh Reynolds /AP Photo/Pool

He also testified that the two had exchanged several phone calls after 5 p.m., two from Patrick that Clancy did not answer and one from Clancy where they talked for around 14 seconds.

Reddington began his cross-examination of Chiappini around noon, where he asked Chiappini about Clancy's texts and search history. Reddington asked if Chiappini remembered several searches on Clancy's phone, including "How to slit your throat to die?" "Can you turn airbags off on Kia Sorento?"

"I don't recall," Chiappini said.

Reddington told Chiappini that Clancy did search for those questions, but Chiappini did not locate them during the forensic analysis of her phone.

"Do you recall, sir, that there was also a search for schizophrenia?" Reddington asked. "Not specifically," Chiappini answered. "How about psychosis? Did she search for psychosis as well?"

"There is a keyword search and a Google search," Chiappini said, referring to documents provided by Reddington.

During the cross-examination, Chiappini was asked to read through a series of searches from Clancy's phone, including one from Jan. 19, 2023 about hallucinations. Reddington also asked Chiappini to read through text messages between Patrick and Clancy from Jan. 24, 2023, including one from Patrick that said: "You're a good Mamma."

Chiappini finished his testimony just after 1 p.m. and the jury took a lunch break.

Joshua McKelligan, a Massachusetts State Police officer in the homicide unit, took the stand after lunch. McKelligan went to the Clancys' home in the early morning hours of Jan. 25, 2023, to look around. He was shown pictures and videos from the prosecution of the state of the house, including blood spatter.

McKelligan also testified that he knew that Clancy was on psychiatric meds at the time and included it in the search warrant for the home. His testimony concluded after 20 minutes and a brief cross-examination from Reddington.

Court ended early on Thursday and there will be no testimony on Friday.

Sullivan told jurors to "take these next couple days and rest up. It's been a long couple of weeks." Seventy witnesses have testified so far as the prosecution gets closer to the end of its list.

Commonwealth asks to speak with doctor and priest

After testimony ended on Friday, the Commonwealth asked for the records of people who have spoken with Lindsay Clancy during the trial, including a priest and medical staff such as psychologist Dr. Paul Zeizel.

Sullivan declined to allow the Commonwealth access to records involving the Roman Catholic priest, but agreed to allow information on Dr. Zeizel.

Lindsay Clancy trial

Clancy, 36, has pleaded not guilty to first-degree murder in the deaths of her three children, 5-year-old Cora, 3-year-old Dawson and 8-month-old Callan, in their Duxbury home on Jan. 24, 2023.

Prosecutors Jennifer Sprague and Shanan Buckingham said Clancy planned the murders before faking a suicide attempt. Reddington said she admits to killing her children, but noted she should not be held criminally responsible because she was overmedicated and suffering from postpartum psychosis.

Several jurors were seen crying Wednesday as autopsy photos were shown. Judge William Sullivan sent the jury out of the courtroom twice Wednesday afternoon as Clancy sobbed loudly during testimony about her children.

Clancy faces life in prison without parole if she's convicted of first-degree murder. If the jury finds that she was not criminally responsible for the deaths of her children, she will be sent to a state psychiatric hospital in Massachusetts.

If you or someone you know is in emotional distress or a suicidal crisis, you can reach the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline by calling or texting 988. You can also chat with the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline here.

For more information about mental health care resources and support, The National Alliance on Mental Illness HelpLine can be reached Monday through Friday, 10 a.m. to 10 p.m. ET, at 1-800-950-NAMI (6264) or email info@nami.org.

World.title: Luigi Mangione in discussions about possible guilty plea, sources say
World.content:
Luigi Mangione, accused in the 2024 killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson, is in discussions about a possible plea deal on federal charges ahead of a court appearance Friday in New York City, sources familiar with the matter told CBS News.

Mangione, 28, is set to appear at an 11 a.m. conference in U.S. District Court in Manhattan. That meeting is taking place after prosecutors and the defense team sent a letter to federal court Tuesday requesting Friday's conference. CBS News New York's Alice Gainer will be inside the courtroom Friday with the latest developments.

Plea discussions between federal prosecutors and defense attorneys have been ongoing and it's unclear if an agreement has been reached, sources told CBS News.

"I expect plea negotiations to happen in every case, or certainly most cases," legal expert Richard Schoenstein said.

Attorneys for Mangione have not responded to CBS News New York's request for comment. A spokesperson for the U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York also declined to comment.

Mangione faces both federal and state charges in connection with Thompson's death. He has pleaded not guilty in both trials.

The federal charges carry a potential maximum life sentence, which Mangione could still face even if a federal plea deal is reached.

"In the federal system, you don't agree to a sentence as part of a plea deal. You agree to a plea and the crime, and then it has to go to a sentencing hearing in front of the judge," Schoenstein said.

If a plea deal is reached, it could have an impact on his state trial, which is set to begin next month. That's because of potential double jeopardy concerns. Double jeopardy refers to a law which says "a person may not be twice prosecuted for the same offense," although a number of exceptions are listed.

"I would expect the defense to make some sort of motion to preclude further prosecution of the state case on the grounds that it is double jeopardy," Schoenstein said. "I think the question of whether or not it would be double jeopardy is open and complicated and subject to debate."

That's because the federal charges have to do with stalking and interstate charges, whereas the state charges are for second degree murder, a weapons charge, and a forged instrument charge.

"So the weapons and forged instrument charges would not be resolved by the federal plea, and arguably the intentional killing charge would not be resolved. I do think there's a serious question as to whether this would be double jeopardy," Schoenstein said.

Schoenstein said a federal plea deal would "put some pressure on state prosecutors to reach a deal of their own, or to become part of the deal that is being negotiated between the feds and the defendant, and therefore it could resolve the case on a negotiated level."

Schoenstein said it could also impact the defense strategy if the state case does go forward, "because if it does go forward he no longer has to worry about a federal trial down the road."

The start of his federal trial, if it moves forward, is set for January.

World.title: "CBS Sunday Morning" launches new series of live events at the 92nd Street Y in NYC, debuting with Sylvester Stallone
World.content:
"CBS Sunday Morning" and the 92nd Street Y in New York City are presenting a new series of conversations featuring the biggest newsmakers in the arts, politics and more before a live audience. "CBS Sunday Morning at 92NY" will kick off on Monday, Sept. 28, at 6 p.m. with correspondent Tracy Smith talking with three-time Academy Award nominee Sylvester Stallone.

CBS News

Smith will talk with Stallone (star of "Tulsa King" on Paramount+) about his career, the creation of "Rocky," his life, and his new memoir, "The Steps." She will preview the event and profile Stallone on the Sept. 27 edition of "Sunday Morning."

"CBS Sunday Morning at 92NY" is the first in an ongoing series of conversations that "Sunday Morning" will present in collaboration with 92NY. It also marks an exciting brand extension for America's #1 Sunday morning news program, which has been best-in-class for 23 seasons and counting.

"Our viewers are passionate about our show and always ask for more," said Rand Morrison, executive producer of "Sunday Morning." "This is a way to bring what makes 'CBS Sunday Morning' special – fascinating, deep conversations with interesting newsmakers – to more people on additional platforms."

William Morrow

"For over 150 years, the 92nd Street Y has been a world-class beacon for culture, deep conversation, and intellectual curiosity," said 92NY CEO Seth Pinsky. "We are honored to work with 'CBS Sunday Morning' on this incredible new programming series. By bringing two great American institutions together, we are creating the kind of deeply engaging experiences our communities crave and expect."

"CBS Sunday Morning at 92NY" will stream live online at www.92ny.org and be featured later on CBSSundayMorning.com, YouTube and Paramount+. Highlights will be featured across "CBS Sunday Morning"'s social media feeds. Additionally, "CBS Sunday Morning" will preview the interviews on the broadcast leading up to every "CBS Sunday Morning at 92NY" event.

Tickets for the first "CBS Sunday Morning at 92NY" are on sale today, Aug. 13, at www.92ny.org.

"CBS Sunday Morning" is broadcast Sundays (9:00-10:30 a.m. ET) on the CBS Television Network and streaming on Paramount+. Rand Morrison is the executive producer.

Follow "CBS Sunday Morning" on X, Facebook, Instagram and at CBSNews.com. Listen to "CBS Sunday Morning" podcasts here and on all podcast platforms. Stream "CBS Sunday Morning" on Paramount+.
