World.title: Georgian Constitutional Court judge issues dissenting opinion on cases involving protests on pavements
World.content:
Judge on protests on pavements in Georgia

A dissenting opinion by Constitutional Court judge Giorgi Kverenchkhiladze has been published on the punishment of people for holding protests on pavements.

Kverenchkhiladze believes that imposing administrative detention on people for peaceful protests and assemblies could cause harm that may later prove impossible to remedy.

The Tbilisi City Court began hearing the so-called “pavement cases” in December 2025. Since January 2026, dozens of demonstrators have faced administrative detention for holding protests on the pavement outside parliament.

Several people petitioned the Constitutional Court to challenge the ban on protests on pavements. They also asked the court to suspend the disputed provisions until it issued a final ruling. The Constitutional Court began hearing the cases but refused to suspend the provisions. Judge Giorgi Kverenchkhiladze believes the court should have suspended them.

However, according to lawyer Giorgi Burdjanadze, Kverenchkhiladze was in the minority among the judges of the Constitutional Court’s First Chamber when they considered the issue.

Judge Giorgi Kverenchkhiladze’s dissenting opinion

“If the threat of administrative detention or imprisonment forces a person to repeatedly refrain from taking part in an assembly or publicly expressing their position, that opportunity can no longer be restored,” the judge wrote.

He said this was why such a restriction could cause “irreparable harm”.

Giorgi Kverenchkhiladze’s dissenting opinion also includes arguments that lawyers raised before the Tbilisi City Court when it considered cases related to protests on pavements. However, the judges did not take those arguments into account.

One such argument concerns the temporary disruption of people’s normal movement in their daily lives.

Judge Giorgi Kverenchkhiladze

Kverenchkhiladze notes that pedestrian movement on pavements can be disrupted for various reasons, including parking violations, commercial or construction activities, and other circumstances. However, the state has never considered imprisonment a necessary measure to protect freedom of movement in such cases.

“Temporary restrictions on pedestrians’ freedom of movement do not represent an interest for which a democratic state would normally resort to imprisonment as a means of protection,” the judge wrote.

Kverenchkhiladze also drew attention to the severity of the sanction. He said harsh punishment not only demonstrates the state’s attitude towards a particular action, but can also discourage people from taking part in protests altogether.

“The severity of the sanction provided for by the disputed provisions indicates not only the degree to which the act is considered reprehensible, but also the strength of the ‘deterrent effect’ it may have on the exercise of freedom of expression and freedom of assembly,” Kverenchkhiladze stressed.

Context

Georgia has seen continuous protests since 28 November 2024. Thousands of people took to the streets after Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze of the Georgian Dream party announced that the government would not put EU accession talks on the agenda for the next four years.

Since then, Georgian Dream has repeatedly restricted freedom of expression through new laws. These measures have included bans on wearing masks and using pyrotechnics at rallies, as well as criminal liability for repeatedly blocking roads during protests.

The most far-reaching of these repressive legislative initiatives came with amendments banning assemblies on pavements. Under the new rules, organisers of any assembly or demonstration on a pavement must notify the Interior Ministry five days before the event. The ministry can also propose an alternative time and location for the protest.

The new rules also introduce administrative detention as the initial penalty for violations, except in certain special cases.

Judge on protests on pavements in Georgia

World.title: ‘We have proved that Armenia is not a province, but a crossroads’ — Pashinyan
World.content:
Pashinyan on EAEU membership and railway concession

Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan said there should be no situation in which anyone could say: “Armenia has nowhere to go and nobody needs it.” Four years ago, Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko made a similar statement.

According to Pashinyan, Lukashenko’s words actually reflect a “deeply rooted institutional perception” of Armenia, not only in Belarus but also in other countries that belong to the Russian-led Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU). The prime minister sees this as a “disrespectful perception”. He believes it developed from the following assumption:

“There is the Karabakh conflict, there is a conflict with Azerbaijan, there is a conflict with Turkey, and this hostility is insurmountable. So they have nowhere to go, and we can treat them however we want.”

However, Pashinyan said Armenia had managed to prove otherwise:

“We have demonstrated in practice that many countries need Armenia as a responsible partner in the international community and as a very important country. We have proved that Armenia is not a province, but a crossroads — together with the South Caucasus and the wider region.”

At a briefing, the prime minister again answered questions about Armenia’s choice between the EAEU and the European Union. He also discussed possible decisions on the management of Armenia’s railways, which Russia took over under a concession agreement in 2008. The Armenian government has effectively developed new proposals that would limit Russia’s role but would not yet terminate its concession.

“Before alternatives emerge, we need both the EU and the EAEU equally”

Russia continues to pressure Armenia over the need to choose between the EAEU and the EU. Armenian journalists therefore asked the government again about its position. Pashinyan said Russia expected Armenia to choose between “two alternatives”. However, the “second alternative” has not yet taken shape:

“We will certainly make this choice through a referendum in the future. But this will happen only after we first carry out the necessary institutional preparations and then formally apply for EU membership.”

According to Pashinyan, Armenia currently needs both the EU and the EAEU equally because the second alternative does not yet exist. He also said Armenia could eventually face not only a choice between these two options, but also a third approach:

“Perhaps a third initiative will emerge: neither the EAEU nor the EU. In other words, we do not need either structure. Who said that everyone must belong to some structure?”

Moreover, he said the government was considering many possible options, including “a fourth and fifth alternative”.

Returning to the issue of holding a referendum on EAEU or EU membership, he stressed:

“This choice must be a mature one because we do not yet know how realistic this path is or what the roadmap will look like.”

Without naming Russia, the prime minister said Armenia could not treat anyone’s interests with contempt or disregard. But it also could not put another country’s interests above its own national interests.

“That is why we are trying to discuss and resolve all issues patiently, without escalation or nervousness. We will discuss them for as long as necessary, until we find a solution that more or less satisfies both sides,” he said.

“We will not pursue the termination of the concession agreement”

Nikol Pashinyan once again said Yerevan wanted to resolve the issue of Armenia’s railway “in a friendly manner” without escalating the situation. He said both Armenia and Russia should consider each other’s interests and seek compromises.

This time, the prime minister outlined several possible scenarios for how the situation could develop:

“One of them could involve the Russian side selling its concession rights, either fully or partially. In other words, there could be certain shareholder configurations,” he said.

According to Pashinyan, Armenia does not want to terminate the concession agreement. It has always had that option and still does. However, the Armenian side prefers not to take such measures.

He said a possible solution for Yerevan would involve a Russian company selling its concession rights to a third party at market value.

At the same time, he noted that this approach might not be particularly acceptable to Russia’s partners.

He also said the Armenian government was working with experts to find an option that would at least partly address the concerns of both sides:

“[The experts] say that we could introduce a different management model. For example, Russia could retain part of its shares while transferring the rest. But the Russian side would have to retain a smaller stake. Otherwise, the problem would not be resolved.

There is another idea. The licence could be divided into two parts. At present, the railway infrastructure and its operation form a single package.”

Pashinyan explained the problems facing Armenia:

“The current situation prevents Armenia from seizing the historic opportunity to integrate our railway into the international rail network.”

He noted that countries responsible for the “lion’s share” of rail freight and which could become potential beneficiaries are looking for ways to bypass Armenia:

“They not only tell us this, but we can also see that they are showing no investment interest in this sector. As a result, we understand that the reason lies in the fact that our railway is under a Russian concession.”

Nikol Pashinyan added that this was why the government had raised the issue with its Russian partners in a friendly manner and proposed finding solutions.

Since 2008, Armenia’s railways have operated under a concession held by South Caucasus Railway. The company is a wholly owned subsidiary of Russian Railways. The agreement provides for a 30-year concession. However, since 2008, freight volumes have halved, some routes have stopped operating, and the required investments have remained on paper. Meanwhile, Armenia wants to fully unblock its borders, which requires restoring railway links to the borders with Azerbaijan and Turkey. Since the Russian company that operates Armenia’s railways has not undertaken to restore these sections, Armenia is looking for ways to implement the plans itself.

Pashinyan on EAEU membership and railway concession

World.title: Fuel supplies from Tbilisi-controlled territory to Abkhazia: humanitarian aid or move in Russia’s interests?
World.content:
Fuel supplies to Abkhazia

Amid a severe fuel shortage in Abkhazia, the import of fuel from territory controlled by Tbilisi has sparked political controversy. The government says a private company delivered the shipment in full compliance with Georgian law, while the opposition and critics are calling for further clarification and answers to several questions: where did the fuel go, who brought it into Abkhazia, and for what purpose?

At a briefing on 12 August 2026, Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze confirmed that fuel had reached Abkhazia from territory controlled by Georgia. He said the government had not organised the operation and that private companies had imported the fuel in accordance with the law.

According to ruling-party MP Rati Ionatamishvili, the shipment amounted to 3,000 tonnes of fuel, delivered to Abkhazia by several tankers. He said the shipment reached Abkhazia while fully respecting Georgia’s sovereignty and legislation.

Ionatamishvili criticised the opposition for its focus on the deliveries and dismissed as absurd suggestions that the operation aimed to supply Russia with several thousand tonnes of fuel. He said the 3,000 tonnes delivered to Abkhazia represented a negligible share of Russia’s annual fuel consumption. He added that presenting the issue in this way served a campaign aimed at undermining efforts to restore Georgian-Abkhaz relations.

Above all, the opposition is demanding details that the government has not yet provided.

According to Levan Samushia, one of the leaders of the Strong Georgia – Lelo alliance, the prime minister’s statement that the fuel was imported in compliance with the Law on Occupied Territories is not enough:

“Who supplied the fuel — in other words, where did it come from — and who was the recipient? Were Georgia’s laws and national interests respected?”

He said it was necessary to know which commercial entities were involved and what route the fuel took to reach Abkhazia.

Levan Samushia

Similar questions have also been raised by Berdia Sichinava, one of the leaders of the Gakharia – For Georgia party. However, he stressed that if the fuel shipment was genuinely humanitarian and did not violate the law, there was no problem with providing such assistance in itself.

“Georgia is involved in more than one such humanitarian project. For example, we fund medical treatment for our citizens from Abkhazia, we receive electricity from the Enguri Hydroelectric Power Plant, and people living in the occupied territory also receive it,” Sichinava said.

In his view, the main problem is the lack of transparency surrounding the process. Sichinava is demanding clarification on who imported the fuel, how large the shipment was, what procedures the cargo went through and where it was ultimately delivered.

Sichinava considers the way the fuel was ultimately used a particularly important question: did it go towards the needs of Abkhazia’s population and critical infrastructure, or was it eventually used in Russia-controlled areas to the south, including infrastructure linked to military activities?

“If the fuel entered occupied Abkhazia as a commercial rather than humanitarian shipment, and if it went through so-called customs procedures at the so-called border — which is actually the occupation line — this could raise serious concerns for our country’s territorial integrity and security,” Sichinava said.

Lasha Parulava, a member of the United National Movement, accused the government of serving Russian interests and betraying Georgia’s national interests.

He called Kobakhidze’s statement that the fuel deliveries complied with the Law on Occupied Territories cynical. Parulava also criticised the government’s policy towards Russia and noted that the fuel was supplied to Abkhazia amid a fuel shortage in Russia itself.

“This is not simply aiding the enemy, but a direct betrayal of national interests,” Parulava said.

Lasha Parulava

Nika Gvaramia, leader of the Coalition for Change, believes the government may have authorised the operation in advance, although the public has not been told why, when or on what grounds it approved it.

Gvaramia points out that Russian military bases are deployed in Abkhazia and that the Russian military is facing fuel shortages.

In his view, these circumstances make it necessary to establish whether humanitarian or social considerations genuinely prompted the fuel shipment, or whether Russia ultimately used the cargo for military purposes.

Gvaramia argues that, in that case, the issue would go beyond the legality of economic activity in Georgia’s occupied territory. The situation could also involve the supply of goods of strategic importance to Russia.

Nika Gvaramia

Expert Gia Khukhashvili assesses the volume of fuel and the logistics of its delivery differently from the authorities. In his view, the “several tankers” mentioned by government officials actually represent a much larger shipment.

“Three thousand tonnes is a convoy of at least 100 fuel tankers,” Khukhashvili wrote.

He said fuel deliveries to Abkhazia could theoretically mark the beginning of a reintegration process. Under the current government, however, he described the decision as “an act of collaborationism and sheer greed”.

Tamta Mikeladze, director of the Social Justice Center, wrote:

“Amid Russia’s economic weakening, Abkhazia may need support from Tbilisi, and this crisis could provide an opportunity to transform the conflict.

Any step that could benefit the people of Abkhazia should not automatically be seen as serving Russia’s interests. That is precisely why full transparency is necessary: who makes the decision, what is its purpose, what mechanisms are in place to monitor the process so that it does not strengthen Russia’s military and economic interests, and what political strategy accompanies it?

Meeting humanitarian or civilian needs and strengthening Russia’s interests are not the same thing. However, a lack of transparency can blur the distinction and turn such actions into part of Russia’s game.

The particular problem with the Abkhaz issue is that a crisis can become an opportunity only if there is a political vision. Georgian Dream has no such vision. The party has yet to adopt either a de-occupation plan or strategic documents for rebuilding trust.

Irakli Kobakhidze has not even attempted to answer the questions raised above.

Given the deep mistrust of Georgian Dream and the complete lack of transparency surrounding its policies, concerns that something could happen that fundamentally and permanently contradicts our national interests are entirely understandable. However, accuracy and attention to nuance are crucial when formulating criticism.”Fuel supplies to Abkhazia (civil.ge)

Fuel supplies to Abkhazia

World.title: EU annual report: “serious problems” in Azerbaijan and “serious restrictions” on fundamental freedoms
World.content:
European Union annual report

The EU says that the human rights and democracy situation in Azerbaijan in 2025 continued to be marked by “serious problems”. It highlighted restrictions on civil society and media freedom, concerns about the independence of the judiciary, and limited progress on structural reforms.

The overall situation in governance remained restrictive. This is according to the European Union’s Annual Report on Human Rights and Democracy in the World for 2025.

The report says legislative, administrative and judicial mechanisms “seriously restrict” the exercise of fundamental freedoms.

At the same time, the assessment notes progress in several areas. These include the criminalisation of child marriage, new measures to promote gender equality, and efforts to combat corruption.

The EU’s assessment of Azerbaijan in 2025 is critical but balanced.

Civil society under pressure

In 2025, civil society organisations continued to operate under restrictive conditions.

The EU notes that the 2017 Law on Non-Governmental Organisations remains in force. Registration, reporting and grant approval requirements continue to restrict the activities of independent organisations.

Local organisations reported persistent administrative pressure and increased scrutiny.

The departure of several UN agencies, including the United Nations Development Programme and UNICEF, also affected their operating environment. This reduced opportunities for international monitoring and assistance.

The EU says it continues to support civil society, independent media and human rights defenders, including through human rights monitoring and legal assistance programmes for vulnerable groups.

Concerns over the judiciary and the rule of law

According to the EU, problems related to the rule of law and judicial independence persist.

The assessment says courts lack sufficient independence when handling politically sensitive cases.

The report cites judgments by the European Court of Human Rights as an important indicator of the problems that remain.

In 2025, the ECHR issued 39 judgments in cases concerning Azerbaijan and found violations in 38 of them. Most cases involved the right to a fair trial, deprivation of liberty, freedom of expression and freedom of assembly.

The report also notes that Azerbaijan’s failure to implement ECHR judgments has affected the country’s relations with the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe.

Electoral system remains unchanged

The EU notes that Azerbaijan’s electoral system underwent no changes in 2025.

The country did not carry out major reforms aimed at implementing the long-standing recommendations of the OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights and the Council of Europe’s Venice Commission.

The report identifies the lack of progress in this area as one of the persistent challenges to Azerbaijan’s democratic development.

Progress in some areas

The EU report also notes a number of legislative changes.

In July 2025, Azerbaijan criminalised child marriage.

The authorities approved a National Action Plan on Gender Equality for 2026–2028 and amended the Law on Combating Corruption.

The amendments include provisions on whistleblower protection and corruption risk management.

At the same time, the EU notes that the implementation of these measures remains uneven.

Dialogue continues, reforms remain limited

Throughout 2025, the EU maintained regular contacts with the Azerbaijani authorities.

These included meetings with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the Office of the Ombudsman and the State Committee for Work with Religious Organisations.

The discussions covered judicial reform, media freedom, the treatment of people in detention, the rights of religious minorities, gender equality and the fight against corruption.

The EU also raised concerns about individuals who had been arrested or barred from leaving the country for exercising their fundamental rights.

Human rights issues also featured in sectoral dialogues on public administration, justice and social policy.

However, despite the continued channels of engagement, the EU says that “progress on structural reforms remains limited”.

Media freedom and fundamental rights

Media freedom and freedom of expression remained among the areas closely monitored by the EU.

The report notes that throughout the year, the EU closely monitored developments concerning digital rights, freedom of expression and media freedom.

EU-funded programmes supported independent media, human rights monitoring, legal assistance, gender equality and children’s rights.

The EU continued to support civil society organisations and human rights defenders working under restrictive conditions.

Azerbaijan on international platforms

The EU continued to raise human rights concerns in Azerbaijan through international organisations.

At the UN, during the 80th session of the General Assembly’s Third Committee, the EU raised issues concerning the space for civil society, judicial independence and media freedom.

Cooperation with the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights also continued, including preparations for Azerbaijan’s next Universal Periodic Review, scheduled for 2026–2027.

Within the Council of Europe, the EU supported mechanisms for implementing ECHR judgments and engaged with the Venice Commission and the Commissioner for Human Rights.

At the OSCE, the EU and its member states took part in discussions on media freedom and electoral standards, including restrictions affecting the work of the Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights.

European Union annual report

World.title: ‘Even if nuclear power plant is shut down, Armenia will not face serious problems’: Reaction to Aliyev’s remarks
World.content:
Yerevan reacts to Aliyev’s AzTV interview

“Every nuclear power plant has an operating lifespan. Neither the Armenian government nor the Azerbaijani government, nor the government of any other country in the world, determines that lifespan,” Armenian ruling-party MP Arman Yeghoyan said in response to the Azerbaijani president’s remarks.

In an interview with AzTV, Ilham Aliyev said the Metsamor Nuclear Power Plant was “outdated” and posed a potential threat to the entire region. He said “sooner or later it must be shut down”, after which “Armenia will face a full-scale energy crisis”.

At the same time, the Azerbaijani president said an energy corridor running through Armenia to Nakhchivan, then to Turkey and Europe, would “allow Armenia’s energy system to withstand a crisis”.

MP Arman Yeghoyan responded that “Aliyev has not made any revelation”. The maximum permitted operating period of the nuclear power plant expires in 2036, a fact that has long been known.

“And we have already announced that we are considering building a new nuclear power plant and are negotiating with several international partners,” the MP said.

Political analyst Samvel Meliksetyan believes Azerbaijan is trying to portray itself as a “generous country ready to help Armenia solve its problems”, despite the long-running conflict.

He noted that this was not the first such case. Baku had previously said that Azerbaijan could serve as a reliable partner for supplying energy resources to Armenia. Meliksetyan, however, said Armenia currently has a surplus of electricity. He stressed that even if the nuclear power plant shuts down, the country will not face serious problems.

“The claim that Armenia’s energy system will face a crisis after the Metsamor Nuclear Power Plant closes is not true,” the political analyst told JAMnews.

He said Armenia does not currently need additional sources of electricity. He noted that the project for a new nuclear power plant remains under discussion and that Armenia has opportunities to expand solar power.

In addition, the fifth unit of the Hrazdan Thermal Power Plant has roughly the same generating capacity as the nuclear plant. The only problem is that the nuclear power plant produces cheaper electricity.

Aliyev again refers to TRIPP as the “Zangezur Corridor”

During his visit to Nakhchivan, Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev gave an interview to state broadcaster AzTV. Alongside the issue of the nuclear power plant’s closure, Aliyev discussed the 2020 Second Karabakh War. He called the trilateral statement of 9 November, which ended the fighting, “an act of Armenia’s capitulation”. He added that “there is no need to look for any humiliating or offensive meaning in this term; it is simply a reality”.

He then turned to the issue of transport links between mainland Azerbaijan and Nakhchivan. He stressed that this route had remained one of Baku’s strategic goals for many years.

“On 9 November, trilateral negotiations took place with the mediation of the Russian president. I insisted categorically that the statement we were about to sign must include a corridor linking mainland Azerbaijan with the Nakhchivan Autonomous Republic. The Armenian side did not want to agree to this. But it did not have many alternatives. If the war had continued, we would of course have suffered losses as well, but Armenia’s losses would have been much greater. Its troops were, so to speak, surrounded, and their destruction had effectively become a possibility,” the president said.

Point 9 of the November [statement], which the leaders of Armenia, Azerbaijan and Russia signed, does not refer only to a road linking Azerbaijan with Nakhchivan. It states: “All economic and transport links in the region shall be unblocked.” Moreover, the document does not contain the term “corridor”.

Aliyev went on to say that Armenia had delayed implementation of the relevant provision of the 9 November statement and had taken no practical steps to create the “Zangezur Corridor”.

According to him, Russia, the third signatory to the statement, either could not ensure its implementation or had other reasons for not doing so.

“Until August last year, this issue remained frozen. The situation changed when the United States became involved, around spring 2025. The implementation of the project known as TRIPP then began successfully,” Aliyev said, linking the Trump Route transit project to the idea of the “Zangezur Corridor”.

For several years, Baku had demanded that Armenia provide a “Zangezur Corridor” to connect Azerbaijan with Nakhchivan. The Armenian authorities repeatedly said they were ready to unblock all transport links, but refused to provide a “corridor”. The issue stemmed from the fact that Azerbaijan used the term “corridor” to refer to an extraterritorial route. Armenia, meanwhile, refused to give up sovereign control over its own territory.

On 8 August 2025, the sides reached an agreement in Washington, with the mediation of the US president, under which Armenia would provide a route while retaining its sovereign rights. The transit project therefore received the name “Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity” (TRIPP).

Aliyev also said that, as part of TRIPP, Azerbaijan had already prepared a project to build power transmission lines from mainland Azerbaijan to Nakhchivan through Armenian territory:

“As a result of our specialists’ survey of Armenian territory, we identified the points where the supporting pylons should be installed.”

The Azerbaijani president expressed hope that “Armenia will not delay this process”, saying it would also benefit the country.

“There is no infrastructure by that name in Armenia” — MP

Arman Yeghoyan, an MP from Armenia’s ruling Civil Contract party, said that documents signed by Armenia and Azerbaijan, including the peace agreement initialled in Washington, do not contain the term “Zangezur Corridor”.

“At the level of political narratives, you can say many things. But we are saying that there is no such concept or infrastructure with such a name or term on Armenian territory.”

The MP urged people to remember that Armenia is implementing the TRIPP project. The leaders of Armenia, Azerbaijan and the United States signed the declaration launching the project in Washington on 8 August 2025.

Comment

According to political analyst Samvel Meliksetyan, when the Azerbaijani side explains what it means by the “Zangezur Corridor”, it refers to the railway from Horadiz to Nakhchivan and then on to Turkey. He also noted that Aliyev used the name TRIPP in his interview.

The analyst said the meaning attached to the term “Zangezur Corridor” in 2022–2023 differs from what it means today. In his assessment, the project no longer involves an extraterritorial corridor:

“From a legal standpoint, TRIPP cannot become an extraterritorial corridor. But from a propaganda standpoint, Azerbaijan uses and will continue to use the term ‘Zangezur Corridor’, with some modifications.”

Meliksetyan stressed that the “Trump Route” project would proceed according to principles agreed with US mediation.

Commenting on Aliyev’s statement about building power transmission lines through Armenian territory, the political analyst said the sides were assessing the most suitable routes. He said the involvement of Azerbaijani specialists should not be interpreted as “acting on their own”.

“All the work is being carried out within the TRIPP framework. An electricity link will run through Armenian territory and connect the two parts of Azerbaijan. Azerbaijani specialists can only discuss where the link will enter Armenia from Azerbaijani territory and where it will re-enter Azerbaijan,” the expert explained.

Summing up his impressions of Aliyev’s interview, Meliksetyan said the Azerbaijani president had spoken in his characteristic style, seeking to highlight his “political achievements”.

The analyst said it was no coincidence that Aliyev focused on Nakhchivan’s economic and energy development, as well as its transport prospects. The president said Azerbaijan would finance the railway restoration itself, but also expressed interest in attracting international investors.

“Although Azerbaijan has repeatedly said that it has no financial problems, they certainly exist. Baku is trying to attract new investment to Nakhchivan through TRIPP to restore this section of the railway,” Meliksetyan said.

Yerevan reacts to Aliyev’s AzTV interview

World.title: Severe petrol shortages hit Abkhazia amid Russia fuel crisis following Ukrainian attacks — VIDEO
World.content:
Fuel shortages in Abkhazia

Severe fuel shortages continue in Abkhazia in the middle of the tourist season. All petroleum products are supplied exclusively from Russia, leaving one clear explanation: fuel shortages in Russia caused by Ukrainian drone attacks on oil and gas facilities.

The Abkhaz authorities are holding emergency talks with Moscow and say progress has been made. Reports say Russia has already arranged for 1,600 tonnes of AI-92 petrol to be sent to Abkhazia, with the first shipment expected to arrive in the coming days.

For now, petrol is available only at Rosneft and Podorozhnik filling stations.

Meanwhile, reports say petrol was supplied from territory controlled by Tbilisi

Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze confirmed this:

“Amid the severe fuel shortage, a shipment was made to Abkhazia, but it was not supplied by the state, it was supplied by private businesses. If we continue to have the opportunity to ease the situation for the people living there, both Georgians and Abkhaz, we will continue to do so,” Kobakhidze said.

The Abkhaz news agency Apsnypress asked the Abkhaz government for comment following Kobakhidze’s statement and received the following response:

“Due to the circumstances caused by external factors, there is not enough motor fuel to meet Abkhazia’s needs. The authorities therefore decided to allow fuel supplies from alternative sources. Fuel market participants managed to arrange a shipment of petrol from Georgian territory. As is well known, Abkhazia also supplied fuel to Georgia from its territory in the post-war 1990s.”

Kobakhidze’s statement drew criticism from the opposition in Tbilisi. Opposition politicians said the fuel supplies to Abkhazia “could in fact mean supplies to Russian military bases”.

Economist and opposition politician Roman Gotsiridze said: “It is possible that the fuel could also have been transported to Russian territory. The company that made these deliveries will not escape sanctions.”

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

Fuel shortages in Abkhazia

World.title: Georgian PM confirms “fuel was supplied to occupied Abkhazia from Tbilisi-controlled territory”
World.content:
Fuel supplies to Abkhazia

Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze confirmed that petrol had been supplied from Tbilisi-controlled territory amid a severe fuel shortage in occupied Abkhazia. A journalist asked Kobakhidze about the issue.

Occupied Abkhazia has recently faced a severe fuel shortage, leading to significant restrictions on supplies of petrol and other petroleum products.

“We did not introduce this; it was introduced by private businesses,” Kobakhidze said at a briefing. He added that such measures were being taken in line with Georgia’s existing legislation, including the Law on Occupied Territories.

He said the Georgian government was ready to help ease the situation for people living in occupied Abkhazia where possible.

“If we can ease the situation, including for the population living in Abkhazia, we will do so, but we will act within the framework of the Law on Occupied Territories,” Kobakhidze said.

Kobakhidze also referred to the government’s “A Step to a Better Future” programme. According to him, it provides support for people living in the occupied territories, including the Abkhaz population.

Comment

Opposition Coalition for Change leader Nika Gvaramia reacted to Kobakhidze’s statement and called on the government to provide further clarification.

Gvaramia noted that Georgia’s Law on Occupied Territories generally prohibits direct unauthorised economic activity in Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region, although it provides certain exceptions, including for activities carried out for humanitarian purposes.

Gvaramia suggested that the fuel supplies in this case could have been intended for Russia’s “war machine”.

Nika Gvaramia: “We are dealing with an action that was presumably authorised by the government in advance. However, the public has not been told the grounds for such authorisation, or when and why it was issued.

“Given that:

— the Russian military machine is facing a severe fuel shortage, while Russian military bases are located in occupied Abkhazia;

— the Ivanishvili regime has repeatedly and deliberately stressed the need for cooperation with Russia;

— taking into account Georgia’s security and territorial integrity interests, as well as Western sanctions imposed on Russia, fuel supplies to territory controlled by Russia cannot be justified on legitimate humanitarian or socio-economic grounds,

“it becomes clear that the Ivanishvili regime has effectively acknowledged that, with its authorisation — and, in essence, by the regime itself — an action is being carried out that runs counter to Georgia’s sovereign interests. It:

violates Georgia’s Constitution;

violates Western sanctions imposed on Russia;

is aimed at assisting the Russian military machine by supplying strategically important products.”

World.title: Baby girl born in driveway of Queensland police station
World.content:
A baby girl has been born in the driveway of a Queensland police station, with officers helping the mother give birth in the back seat of a car.

Officers were returning to the Browns Plains station just after midnight on Tuesday when they were flagged down by a man in a car parked in the driveway.

His 22-year-old heavily pregnant partner was in the car in the late stages of labour, having contractions about two minutes apart.

The couple had been on the way to Logan Hospital, but realised they were not going to make it in time and pulled into the station.

Seven minutes after police arrived, the baby girl was born.

Constable Jenna Ziviani helped deliver her under the guidance of an ambulance officer on the phone.

In vision released by police, Constable Ziviani said it was "super special".

"The operator on the phone was amazing too," she said. "They talk you through it so calmly."

Constable Ziviani said the operator took her through the process, from the baby crowning to supporting the baby's neck and shoulders.

Paramedics arrived shortly after and took the family to hospital.

Police say both are now happy and healthy, recovering at home.

Senior Sergeant Aleisha Young, who arrived shortly after, said it was the first time in her 27-year career she had been on shift for a birth.

"How amazing! " she said.

"It's a celebration, I just don't have champagne to offer you!"

World.title: David McBride had a lot to say as he left jail, but not about whistleblowing
World.content:
David McBride was not planning on speaking to reporters yesterday when he walked free from prison after more than two years behind bars.

But it turns out he had plenty to say from the passenger seat of his pick-up car, driven by family members who hugged him in the sunshine of a crisp Canberra morning.

There was news of a lung cancer diagnosis with surgery in a few weeks, gratitude for the attorney-general who granted him parole, and thanks to hundreds of supporters from across the globe who had sent him letters and cards while locked up.

He also gave a nod to his fellow prisoners, and even the prison staff, who helped make his "hard" time on the inside "a very positive experience … on the whole".

David McBride, who in 2024 was sentenced to five years and eight months in jail, took his assistance dog Jake to court during his trial. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

"I'm looking forward to seeing my dog. And my daughters. But particularly my dog," McBride laughed through the window.

But — perhaps ironically for a whistleblower — it was what went unsaid that piqued interest.

"Any message to whistleblowers, or about whistleblower protection laws?" he was asked by a journalist.

"No, out of respect for the attorney-general I'm not going to say anything political today," he said.

"Though I will at some point talk about those things."

'Don't need to be an angel to be a whistleblower'

He gave this journalist classified military documents. It upended both their lives Military lawyer David McBride gave journalist Dan Oakes more than a hundred classified military documents. Both are still living with the consequences.

McBride's battle began nearly a decade ago when he gave secret defence material to an ABC journalist for the purpose of exposing what he thought was the "over-investigation" of special forces soldiers in Afghanistan.

But the seven-part series his information produced, known as The Afghan Files, instead did the opposite, revealing the alleged involvement of Australian soldiers in unlawful killings.

"… he [Oakes] did do a story on it, but a totally different story to the one, um, that I was pushing", McBride told police in an interview after he was arrested.

This is at the heart of David McBride's complexity — but according to his supporters, the intent should not matter.

David Shoebridge has been one of David McBride's most steadfast supporters. (ABC News: Jerry Rickard)

"You don't need to be an angel to be a whistleblower," Greens senator David Shoebridge, one of McBride's most staunch backers, told reporters on Thursday.

"You don't need to have the world's most perfect motivations.

" At the end of the day, the test is this: if they're letting the public see the truth, well we need to let them speak. "

After pleading guilty to three charges, including theft, the ACT Supreme Court sentenced McBride to five years and eight months imprisonment with a non-parole period of two years and three months.

According to the Human Rights Law Centre, it made him the first person imprisoned over Australia's alleged war crimes in Afghanistan.

Australia's most decorated living soldier, Ben Roberts-Smith, is facing five counts of the war crime of murder after being charged earlier this year, while former SAS soldier Oliver Schulz is facing one count of the same charge.

Whistleblower case outcomes anything but certain

Andrew Wilkie, a former intelligence officer, says David McBride never should have been jailed. (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

Another supporter on Capital Hill, independent MP Andrew Wilkie, said McBride should never have been jailed in the first place.

"The information he provided … was undeniably in the public interest," Mr Wilkie said in a statement.

Before he was the member for Clark, the former intelligence officer famously blew the whistle on faulty intelligence in the lead-up to the Iraq War in 2003, and publicly resigned in protest.

He was never jailed.

Neither was Witness K, a former Australian secret intelligence service agent convicted for conspiring to reveal classified information about a covert operation to bug Timor-Leste's government cabinet room in Dili during oil and gas negotiations.

He pleaded guilty but was handed a three-month suspended sentence.

Bernard Collaery was accused of conspiring with Witness K, but the case was dropped. (ABC News: Nick Haggarty)

His lawyer, former ACT attorney-general Bernard Collaery, was also accused of conspiring with his former client, but his case was dropped with intervention by the then federal attorney-general Mark Dreyfus.

Former tax office employee Richard Boyle exposed the ATO for unethical debt recovery tactics, and despite many of his assertions being substantiated, he was charged and pleaded guilty to four criminal charges.

He faced a maximum prison sentence of 161 years, but, in the end, he was spared convictions, instead receiving a 12-month good behaviour bond.

The outcomes in whistleblower cases are anything but certain, meaning the risk to those considering sharing confidential information in the public interest is so great it remains a deterrent.

David McBride's supporters say whistleblower protections need to be updated to stop similar situations in the future. (Four Corners: Nick Wiggins)

Without legislative changes, McBride's supporters argue, "the exact same scenario could play out again".

"It starts with a whistleblower commission," Senator Shoebridge said.

" It starts with a political will to say that the truth matters. "

The government is considering a dedicated Whistleblower Ombudsman, but is still working through the legislative process.

Plans for a Whistleblower Protection Authority were first floated in 2023, but have since stalled.

Having spent much of the government's lagging consultation time in prison, McBride's looming public calls for reform may have officials wishing they had already delivered their promised overhaul, rather than leaving the door open to the whistleblower poster boy and the advocates that follow him.

World.title: Once-sleepy Sunshine Coast set to build 30-storey skyscraper
World.content:
A developer's plan for a 99-metre tower on the Sunshine Coast has sparked fears about the region's future as the population grows ahead of the 2032 Olympics.

Once a sleepy beachside village, the Sunshine Coast today is a rapidly booming area that now includes an emerging CBD.

But a proposal for a 30-storey high-rise to transform the Maroochydore skyline has triggered some residents' fears that the region could become another Gold Coast.

An artist's impression of the future Maroochydore City Centre, described as Australia's largest greenfield CBD. (Supplied: Walker Corporation)

Sydney developer Walker Corporation has applied to the Queensland government to construct the largest tower on the Sunshine Coast.

The residential building with 200 apartments and penthouses would be in the new city centre, which allows for one "landmark" building up to 100 metres tall.

Residents fear 'start of the end'

Many residents are concerned this new tower could lead to maximum heights increasing down the track.

Peter Cowan from Palmwoods said the region should stay "low-key" and eschew high-rise living seen on the Gold Coast.

"Next minute we're going to have shadows over the beach, people not being able to sunbake between certain hours," he said.

"It's the start of the end.

"We don't need that stuff here; we don't want it."

Nambour resident Jeff Spencer described the proposal as the "thin edge of the wedge".

Kate Harvey and Tracey Goodwin-McDonald (pictured) led M-TAG's campaign against beachfront high-rises. (ABC Sunshine Coast: Amy Sheehan)

"One tall building [now], two and three in 20 years' time. I'm obviously concerned about that," he said.

"It's almost like a developer's paradise with these approvals with the Olympics."

Kate Harvey from Mass Transit Action Group led a successful community campaign against light rail for the Sunshine Coast.

"We're not against growth generally, but we do have to protect our lifestyle here," she said.

"The CBD is probably the most appropriate place to put any increase in density.

"We are not the Gold Coast … we don't want to see wall-to-wall high-rise along the coastal corridor."

Ms Harvey said the alternative to higher density housing was "some degree of urban sprawl".

Business chamber supportive

Maroochydore Chamber of Commerce president Brendan Bathersby said the proposed building was "iconic".

"Don't judge it on what it might look like today if it was built," he said.

"Understand that this is part of the Sunshine Coast that's going to be developed over a period of years."

An artist's impression of a major entertainment centre proposed for the Maroochydore CBD. (Supplied: Walker Corporation)

"Is it different to what's been on the Sunshine Coast forever and a day? Absolutely it is, but don't compare it with Toowoomba or Hervey Bay.

"A building like this … is not comparable to what happens on the Gold Coast.

"We've never going to have that.

"There's a lot of naysayers and I understand a lot of people don't want to see the Sunshine Coast change, but in areas like the city centre that change is going to happen."

The Gold Coast has more than 50 buildings above 100 metres in height.

Benefactor's great-granddaughter 'horrified'

Robyn Lister's family has a historical connection to the land and she said she was "quite horrified" by the proposal.

"My great-grandfather was Robert Horton and he originally donated that land to the Maroochydore people to be used for public use only. That was in about 1930," she said.

Matilda and Robert Horton, the former owners of land that's now the Maroochydore CBD, in a photo from circa 1940. (Supplied: Robyn Lister)

The land became a golf course in 1950, before the council acquired the property for $42 million in 2012.

The state government declared a priority development area in 2013 to take control of planning for the 60-hectare site.

While several medium-rise buildings have been constructed already, the 30-storey tower would be the tallest.

"To think a high-rise like this is going to be built there, to me it's part of my family history that's being lost," Ms Lister said.

"It's the last thing we need on the Sunshine Coast, that's for sure.

"To think that area was originally donated to be used as a green area for the locals … it's disappointing to hear something like that is going to be built on that block."

The Horton Park Golf Club pictured in 2009 before it was acquired by the council in 2012 for the new CBD. (Supplied: Maroochy River Golf Club)

Mayor defends election pledge

A key plank of Sunshine Coast Mayor Rosanna Natoli's election pitch was promising no new high-rises.

"New – meaning nothing that wasn't already planned," she said.

"What we're talking about here is a building in a designated CBD area and that [information] has been out for many, many years.

"If the density and height goes here, it's actually meaning [it won't go] where we don't want it to go, which is along the coastline and in our rural and hinterland areas.

" So it's protecting our lifestyle is the way I think about that. "

Approval for the project sits with the state government, not the council, and it is under consideration.

Deputy Premier and Planning Minister Jarrod Bleijie said he was not aware of the project's status.

But he said the Sunshine Coast could still retain its charm while simultaneously adding much-needed housing supply.

"The best thing we can do for affordability is availability," Mr Bleijie said.

"There are ways to keep the lifestyle of the Sunshine Coast but also provide housing for our children and our grandchildren.

Walker Corporation declined to comment.

World.title: Property lobby calls for stamp duty change for first home buyers
World.content:
First home buyers in three Australian jurisdictions are being slugged tens of thousands of dollars in taxes when buying established homes, as a property industry lobby says now is the time for concessions.

South Australia, Tasmania and the Northern Territory are the only Australian states that do not offer stamp duty waivers or concessions on houses that are not new.

According RevenueSA's stamp duty calculator, a $700,000 established home in SA would cost a first home buyer an additional $32,330 in taxes.

Bruce Djite, South Australian executive director of the Property Council, said stamp duty concessions for established homes should definitely be on the government's agenda now.

"On the back of the federal budget changes recently, clearly investors have vacated the space when it comes to established dwellings, so I think the state government absolutely should look at pulling all levers, as they always tell us, here's a lever that is yet to be pulled," he said.

"Investors aren't buying existing stock, that market has really gone dormant and what a great opportunity for first home buyers to be able to buy something where they've grown up, where their jobs are, where their family is."

Bruce Djite says the South Australian government should allow first home buyers to get stamp duty relief on established houses. (ABC News: Dan Taylor)

SA housing minister Nick Champion said he was against a policy change as adding more demand to existing homes was "an incredibly foolish thing to do".

"It would be idiotic to do that, what we do is give tax concessions to new builds," Mr Champion said.

" It's stupid, other state governments shouldn't do it. "

Young people in favour of reform

Architecture student Clementine Cooke-Hall, 20, was in support of the stamp duty change and said buying a house in Adelaide was "out of the question for most young people".

"If you are on welfare benefits, there would be almost no properties in the entire country that you could afford," she said.

"We need houses to be built for human need instead of profit."

University student Sam Menadue said having to pay stamp duty on established homes was unfair.

He also feared that young people would be forced to move further from the city as they search for new builds.

"By moving young people away you're kind of taking away from the nightlife, all the 20-somethings obviously enjoy Hindley Street so how are they going to do that when they live so far up north they can't get there," he said.

"You got to think about the young people, they're the future of the state, you want them to stay here [in SA]."

Sam Menadue believes Adelaide's nightlife will decline if young people are unable to live near the city. (ABC News: Briana Fiore)

Mr Menadue also said young people were scraping by while saving for a deposit.

"The cost of rent, the cost to pretty much do everything is just not that much fun, even going to the footy is really expensive."

Glenelg renter Jordan Armstrong said students were paying hundreds of dollars to live in "share houses in despicable living conditions".

Mr Armstrong said the entire housing market was "completely rigged for the rich" but "housing should be a human right that everyone has access to".

"People are told you can grow up and be able to get a house one day," he said.

"But the reality is for a whole bunch of people that's not been the case, that the cost-of-living crisis and the housing crisis has meant it's not an option for a whole bunch of people."

Here's how different states and territories assist first home buyers

World.title: Spotlight on granny flat fire safety after Sydney family killed in blaze
World.content:
A "ferocious" blaze that killed a family of three last month in a granny flat has put a spotlight on fire safety amid a boom in smaller dwelling approvals.

Emergency services were called to a residence behind a main property in Sydney's south-west on July 29.

Firefighters discovered the bodies of a 52-year-old man, his 43-year-old wife and their 16-year-old son in the Wiley Park property.

Fire and Rescue NSW (FRNSW) Commissioner Jeremy Fewtrell said at the time the granny flat was "completely destroyed" by fire, with "a number of obstacles" making it difficult for crews.

The granny flat was located behind the main residence. (ABC News)

A later statement released by FRNSW revealed the only entry/exit was the front door, "which was blocked by intense flames".

"The building's four windows were secured with iron bars," the statement said.

While the cause of the fire is still under investigation, the incident has highlighted the importance of fire safety in smaller dwellings.

Granny flat oversight

Secondary dwellings have grown in popularity nationally as costs of land, building and everyday living continues to rise.

"For New South Wales, we saw a 23.6 per cent increase for the 2025-2026 financial year, with over 3,592 approvals for granny flats," Housing Industry Association's (HIA) chief executive of industry and policy, Simon Croft, said.

Granny flats are allowed in designated residential zones under the State Environmental Planning Policy (Housing) 2021, although some councils may allow them in other areas.

While NSW had historically taken the lead "due to their planning rules", Mr Croft said other states were also starting to fast-track approvals.

A HIA 2025 member survey found builders expected there to "likely" be 10 times more granny flats constructed across the country in 2026 than in 2022.

Granny flats are classed as a 1A dwelling under the National Construction Code. (ABC News: Nick Haggarty)

Mr Croft said anyone building or significantly renovating a granny flat had to follow fire safety rules included within the National Construction Code (NCC), which were not retrospectively applied.

He said a building surveyor checks over plans and in most states and territories, mandatory inspections take place throughout, at critical stages, and at the final sign off.

"Then you have other sort of certification of the approval, and the people that undertake the works making declarations of compliance," Mr Croft said.

A NSW Department of Planning, Housing and Infrastructure (DPHI) spokesperson said in a statement granny flats "can be approved by the relevant local council through a development application process, or with a fast-track complying development certificate".

Balancing fire safety and home security

The cause of the Wiley Park blaze is still under investigation. (ABC News)

Mr Croft said the NCC had "very contemporary" fire safety rules that were reviewed and updated multiple times over the past two decades.

It covers access points, location of dwellings and smoke alarm fittings.

A Building Commission NSW spokesperson said granny flats were generally considered a Class 1a dwelling under the code, which meant "they must meet the same core fire and safety requirements as a house".

The NCC requires all Class 1a dwellings "have at least one exit from each storey".

Firefighters found the bodies of three members of the same family inside the property. (ABC News)

However, FRNSW said it was best to have at least two exit options in every room. This can be an issue if windows are barred.

"We strongly encourage and recommend everyone to find that balance between home security and home fire safety, whether it be bars on windows, [or] deadlocked doors and windows," Acting Chief Superintendent of Community Safety and Research, Scott Donohoe, said.

" We need to make sure that you can have, where best possible, two means of escape from every room. "

Acting Chief Superintendent Donohoe said FRNSW had witnessed some residents having difficulties escaping from fires because of security measures, which made having a fire escape plan "critical".

FRNSW continued to urge households to boost fire protection following a fatal fire in a mobile home at a tourist park on the South Coast, during which a man's body was recovered.

A number of compliance checks are carried out for granny flat developments and alterations. (Supplied: Housing Industry Association)

Under the NCC, secondary dwellings must be located at an appropriate distance from the main premises and lot boundary.

Smoke alarms must also be installed between bedrooms and the rest of a granny flat on all storeys, including in hallways leading to bedrooms, and in any storey without them.

If a secondary dwelling is built without the required approvals, or deviates from the approved plans, local councils could take action, which might result in an order to stop using the dwelling, or the demolishment of unauthorised works.

What renters can do

Acting Chief Superintendent Donohoe said tenants in rental properties should speak to their landlord "if they're feeling their safety is compromised by security measures".

He said anyone can register or ask for a free home fire safety visit, where they could receive free home fire safety advice, smoke alarm checks and a free smoke alarm if they do not have one.

This includes for alternative housing arrangements such as granny flats, caravans and sheds.

FRNSW encourages renters to speak to their landlords if they are worried about fire safety. (Supplied: Housing Industry Association)

Under NSW legislation, a landlord is obligated to provide at least one working smoke alarm for their tenants in a hallway outside a bedroom or other suitable location in each storey.

"If the smoke alarm is not working in one of their rental properties, it must be repaired within two business days," Acting Chief Superintendent Donohoe said.

Landlords are required to perform annual checks, install or replace removable batteries each year, and replace smoke alarms within 10 years of manufacture.

There may be different requirements for strata scheme properties.

The FRNSW website says NSW legislation provides a "minimal level of protection" and it recommends owners and occupants consider installing additional smoke alarms so there is one in every bedroom.

World.title: Woolworths dumps Farmers' Own milk brand
World.content:
Supermarket giant Woolworths is phasing out its Farmers' Own milk, which is promoted as giving a "better deal to farmers".

Bottles of the milk have already been removed from shelves in South Australia and will leave supermarkets in Western Australia, Queensland, New South Wales and Victoria by 2027.

Dairy farmer Tim Bale from northern New South Wales helped create the Farmers' Own brand in 2013 and said he was sad it was being discontinued.

"I think the general public want to support farmers, but it's hard when they're going in there and they're seeing a cheaper price [alternative]," he said.

"Unfortunately, when you're dealing with such a big company like [Woolworths], we got lost in the shelf space."

Tim Bale says shoppers want to support farmers. (ABC Rural: Jennifer Nichols)

Woolworths has assured farmers that current supply contracts will be honoured.

"We recently consulted our Farmer's Own dairy suppliers about an upcoming contract expiry," a spokesperson said in a statement.

"We are working closely with our suppliers and will continue to honour our contract terms, which includes an option for farmers to extend the contract for an extra 12 months."

Woolworths has not provided any more details, or information about why it has decided to phase out the brand.

But Mr Bale said it was not making the company enough money.

"The oversupply that wasn't going into Farmers' Own, they were selling that at a loss," he said.

"And as our sales decreased, unfortunately, by lack of marketing … that overproduction at a loss becomes more and more, and then to Woolies, it becomes unviable."

Farmers' Own milk is more expensive than Woolworths' home brand milk. (ABC Rural: Warwick Long)

The specialty milk makes up a very small portion of the market, and while Mr Bale was disappointed, he was more concerned there would not be alternative buyers for suppliers' milk.

"At the moment, nobody wants any more milk," he said.

"It's going be hard for all farmers to hold a price. We've got a couple of farmers now that can't be picked up at all."

Just a 'PR exercise'

Australian Dairy Farmers president Ben Bennett said the Farmers' Own brand was "very much a token exercise" for Woolworths.

"I think they were just doing a bit of a PR sort of situation as opposed to having any credible, significant financial improvement to the dairy industry of Australia," he said.

"They had suppliers across the country, but in all fairness, it was very few."

Ben Bennett says the dairy industry needs more than just token support to reverse its decline. (ABC Rural: Jane McNaughton)

Mr Bennett said the local dairy industry has been in decline for the past 20 years.

"We're quite frankly in a dire situation and it's getting worse," he said.

"We have to do something different … having these little niche brands, patronising us little farmers, well, we've got to look at the bigger issue."

World.title: Tasmanian parliament to probe transparency of Rushy Lagoon sale
World.content:
The sale of Tasmania's largest farm to a UK investment firm will be probed by a state parliamentary committee.

Rushy Lagoon, a 21,745-hectare property in the state's north-east was sold to Gresham House after the sale was vetted by the Foreign Investment Review Board and approved by federal Treasurer Jim Chalmers last month.

Gresham House plans to plant about 12 million radiata pine seedlings across 9,000 hectares of the farm over the next five years.

It is also considering cropping and leasing out parts of the farm for grazing, tourism and mountain biking.

There has been community outcry about the sale, mainly over the pine plantation plans.

Gresham House plans to plant about 12 million radiata pine seedlings across the farm over the next five years. (ABC News: Mitchell Woolnough)

Advocacy body TasFarmers described Mr Chalmers' decision as a "betrayal of Tasmanian agriculture".

The Tasmanian government has been vocal in its opposition to the sale and proposed the parliamentary inquiry.

Primary Industries Minister Gavin Pearce told parliament yesterday that significant questions remained, including whether federal government policies were "inadvertently favouring carbon credit outcomes over ongoing fibre and food production".

He said the inquiry was "not about relegating a decision".

"It's about transparency, it's about accountability, it's about ensuring that Tasmania's interests are properly considered in the future," he said.

Gavin Pearce says the inquiry is about ensuring transparency and accountability over the sale. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

With four independent MPs David O'Byrne, George Razay, Craig Garland and Carlo Di Falco voting with the government to establish the inquiry, it had enough support to pass.

Pine, cattle and tourism for Rushy Lagoon The buyer of Tasmania's largest farm says in addition to the pine plantation it has planned for the property, it's also considering cropping and leasing out parts of the farm for grazing, tourism and mountain biking.

Mr O'Byrne told parliament every inquiry had a level of politics about it, but he said if done well the inquiry could be important for the community affected by the sale.

"At the end of the day no-one can doubt that there is significant community concern and we have a responsibility as legislators, as parliamentarians, as representatives of our community to work through a process to inform our community," he said.

Mr O'Byrne also said farming communities "across the country" were looking at the Rushy Lagoon sale.

Neither Labor nor the Greens supported the motion for the inquiry.

Shane Broad says the inquiry is a "witch hunt" which "won't change a thing". (ABC News: Maren Preuss)

Labor's resources spokesperson Shane Broad said the inquiry was "a complete farce".

"The property [sale] settled on Friday, they can't change the outcome," Mr Broad said.

" Regardless of what people think of the sale, the witch hunt committee the Liberals want to set up will have no power to call federal officials and won't change a thing. "

Greens primary industries spokesperson Tabatha Badger said while she acknowledged there was significant concern about the sale, and the Greens also had questions, a federal parliamentary inquiry would be more appropriate.

World.title: One of Australia's longest-serving editors dies aged 96
World.content:
One of Australia's longest serving journalists and editors has died aged 96, after nearly eight decades of contribution to a local newspaper in Victoria's north-west.

Robin Letts had worked at The Buloke Times at Donald since 1947, and had been editor since 1987.

The family newspaper was started by the Letts family in 1875 and had been passed through generations until it was sold late last year.

For over half of the newspaper's history, Letts had been involved with the paper.

On Thursday The Buloke Times announced Letts had died on Wednesday evening.

"We said goodbye to our beloved editor — the man who always found the words when we couldn't," the post read.

"We'll miss him more than we can express.

" Our hearts are broken. "

'An incredible man'

Before starting at the paper in 1947, he had a short stint in the navy aiming to become a sailor, but life on the ocean was not for Letts and he returned to work with his father, Goff Letts.

He became editor after the death of his father in the 1980s.

A young Robin Letts pictured with his father and then editor Goff Letts circa 1985. (Supplied)

Former Buloke Times journalist Shane O'Shea worked with Letts for over half a century.

"I started as a hand and machine compositor and he's been a mentor, friend to me," O'Shea recalled.

"He started off as my boss and later become a business partner and just an incredible man and his contribution to Donald over the years through his writing, through his interest in every group was phenomenal.

"He's left a legacy that will be impossible to emulate, but it'll last forever."

O'Shea said there were no "gutter tactics" in whatever Letts wrote and everything was always honest, factual and from the heart.

Robin Letts (left) with his son, David, and a picture of their ancestor Godfrey Morgan, who founded the newspaper in 1875. (ABC Landline: Tim Lee)

In 2003, Letts was awarded the Medal of the Order of Australia for his service to the Donald community and for his commitment to the publication of the local newspaper.

Last year, the newspaper celebrated its 150-year milestone.

The newspaper surpassed the Fairfax family as the longest continuous family newspaper dynasty in Australia.

Earlier this year, Letts had a fall at work and was unable to fulfil his role as editor, but he retained the title and was committed to the paper until his death.

Letts was still working six days a week until his fall.

"Everyone respected him, everyone was his friend and he just about knew everyone in town and if you wanted help, Robin was there to give it through the newspaper," O'Shea said.

"I think the newspaper is held in high esteem because it represents the community and Robin was the main face of the newspaper."

'A passionate community man'

Buloke Shire Council mayor Graeme Milne said Letts was a gentleman and would help anyone.

"He was a passionate community man, very much involved in anything to do with Donald and the wider community. He had a real interest in people and a great passion to tell their stories," Cr Milne said.

He said Letts would leave a real legacy in the community and across regional Victoria.

"His family was everything, his work was everything and then it was his community and his love for sport and travel," Cr Milne said.

The Buloke Times has been published in Donald since 1875. (ABC Landline: Tim Lee)

ABC Landline senior reporter Tim Lee interviewed Mr Letts and his son, David Letts, last year for the 150-year milestone of the newspaper.

Lee recalled Letts as a "consummate newspaper man".

"He lives and breathed that job and did it from the time he was 17 until 96," he said.

"He almost wrote his last newspaper editorial from his hospital bed, as his late father did."

Lee said Letts had come from an amazing pedigree stemming all the way back to his grandfather.

According to Lee, Letts's great grandfather came to Australia to report on the Goldfields with a letter of introduction from Charles Dickens.

Rural Press Club of Victoria president Kellie Lazzaro said many were reflecting on Letts's remarkable and enduring legacy.

"More than 70 years at the one paper must be a record-breaking innings for any editor and journalist in regional Australia," Lazzaro said.

Earlier this year the press club presented Letts with a Lifetime Achievement Award for his service to the media industry and to the Donald community.

"I'm just so grateful that our industry broadly was able to recognise Robin in that way, and I know that he was incredibly humbled to receive the award," she said.

"It's not easy being a journalist in a small town, there is nowhere to hide.

"The tributes that are coming through today for Robin Letts show that he has been able to work as a journalist and maintain the respect and admiration of his community whilst doing things like holding people to account, attending sporting events and keeping busy."

World.title: Australia news LIVE: White House confirms Trump held phone call with Albanese; Wong to target Hanson’s call for ‘monoculture’ in national security address
World.content:
Foreign Minister Penny Wong will paint Pauline Hanson’s call for a monoculture as a major threat to national security, making the case that Australia’s diversity is a bulwark against global instability while reaffirming that regional diplomacy is Labor’s top priority.

Wong will argue that her own Malaysian background demonstrates how migrants have enriched Australia and helped it find common ground with other people in the world, also pointing to Burundi refugee Nestory Irankunda and his opening goal of the Socceroos’ recent World Cup campaign.

Her speech comes after a charged debate over multiculturalism was spawned in June by Hanson saying Australia should be monocultural. The One Nation leader later backtracked, saying the diverse Socceroos football team was an example of what she was talking about.

Foreign Minister Penny Wong is expected to issue a warning of the dangers of far-right policies. Dominic Lorrimer

Labor has since worn multiculturalism as a badge of pride as it seeks to counter Hanson’s surging popularity, and Wong’s speech will take this a step further by making the direct link between diversity and successful foreign policy.

“Our multicultural society, along with our economy and our democratic institutions, are essential elements of our resilience and raise the costs for those who seek to coerce us,” Wong will say in a speech to the Lowy Institute today.

World.title: Daly Cherry-Evans didn’t want talk of his future to take the gloss off Roosters’ win. So he waited seven hours
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 Daly Cherry-Evans didn’t want talk of his future to take the gloss off Roosters’ win. So he waited seven hours Christian Nicolussi Updated August 14, 2026 — 6:40am ,first published 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The last thing Daly Cherry-Evans wanted was for his next career move to take any gloss off the Sydney Roosters’ excellent win over the Penrith Panthers. So he waited seven hours. Cherry-Evans will quit the NRL at season’s end before taking up a deal with Hull FC in the Super League. Loading There is a good chance he will head for the northern hemisphere with a second premiership ring, to go with the one he won in his maiden NRL season in 2011 at the Sea Eagles, if he can repeat what he did for the Chooks in their 12-10 epic win over the Panthers.



The halfback was the best player on the field against the Panthers, according to coach Trent Robinson, but did not want to comment about his immediate future, or speculate about reports he was heading to the Super League. “The stuff in the future, I’ll sort it out and talk to you guys about it at another time – I won’t leave you hanging,” Cherry-Evans said. Daly Cherry-Evans was brilliant for the Sydney Roosters. NRL By 6am Friday, Cherry-Evans, who spent his first 15 seasons in the NRL at Manly before having his head turned by Bondi officials, confirmed via a Roosters’ press release he would be joining Hull FC in 2027. “I’ve been incredibly fortunate to have had the career I’ve had so far in the NRL, and I feel like the end of this season will be the right time for me to close that chapter,” Cherry-Evans said.



“Manly will always hold a special place for me and my family. I spent more than 15 years there, made lifelong friendships and was fortunate to experience so much throughout my time at the club. I’ll always be grateful to the people at Manly and the supporters for the role they’ve played in my career. “I still have a real desire to play and compete, so the opportunity to join Hull FC and experience the Super League is something I’m genuinely excited about. “I also wouldn’t have had the career I’ve had without the support of my family. My mum and dad have been a constant support throughout my career and I can’t thank them enough for everything they’ve done for me. “My wife Vessa and our girls have been there with me every step of the way, and I’m incredibly grateful for everything they’ve done and the sacrifices they’ve made along the way. This next chapter is a big move for all of us, so to have their support and for us to experience living in England together is something we’re really looking forward to.” Robinson said after the game he had always been an admirer, so much so that, “I saw him two or three years ago at a charity function, I almost bought his boot for a couple of thousand dollars, but one of my mates got it before me”.



Cherry-Evans moved into outright second for most games played with 373. Cameron Smith’s record 430 games remains safe. Andrew Johns said during the week Cherry-Evans should avoid Hull (or “Hell”, as he described it), and was better off focusing on a new franchise like the Perth Bears. Related Article NRL 2026 DCE-inspired Roosters grab top spot from Penrith in nail-biting win Even the bunker looked favourably upon Cherry-Evans on Thursday night, with a knock-on missed late in the second half, which meant the Panthers had to drop out rather than play the ball on their 20m. Penrith were unimpressed with the decision, as were several commentators. The Roosters host the Wests Tigers next Sunday, followed by games against the Dolphins and South Sydney.



Penrith are still in the title race to their eyeballs, with Dylan Edwards to strip fitter for his first-up run after a shoulder injury, and the likes of Mitch Kenny (ankle/leg) and Casey McLean (hand) to return. The home side could have done with McLean’s X-factor out wide. Paul Alamoti hobbled out of the venue with ice strapped to his left hamstring, which means Blaize Talagi could start in the centres next Thursday against the Storm in Melbourne.
