Tech.title: CBP Workers Allegedly Used Government Databases to Spy on Exes, Crushes, and Colleagues
Tech.content:
Internal records obtained by WIRED reveal how, for years, United States Customs and Border Protection employees and contractors were accused of abusing sensitive government databases for reasons that had nothing to do with their jobs. The records contain hundreds of allegations of misuse of law enforcement databases, including federal agents querying data to look up romantic interests, monitor family members, expose various personal information and, in some cases, provide intelligence to suspected smugglers or drug-trafficking organizations.

Acquired through Freedom of Information Act requests to CBP’s Office of Professional Responsibility and the Department of Homeland Security’s Office of Inspector General, the records reveal the breadth of alleged database abuse by CBP employees spanning more than a decade. As immigration and border authorities expand their surveillance through facial recognition, license plate readers, mobile-device searches, and commercially purchased location information generated by ordinary apps, the sheer range of these records, which date from 2009 through 2022, highlights how US residents can be—and have been—targeted by federal government employees with access to highly sensitive data and powerful tools.

WIRED has made this article free for all to read because it is primarily based on reporting from Freedom of Information Act requests. Please consider subscribing to support our journalism.

In one case, a CBP officer allegedly used government databases to contact a flight attendant. In another, an officer was accused of pulling information from trusted-traveler applications to ask people out. Other CBP employees were accused of providing border-crossing data to someone involved in a “heated divorce.” And yet another DHS employee allegedly used controversial ad-tech-derived location data to track several coworkers’ cell phones—which appears to be the first known internal abuse case involving DHS use of ad-tech-derived mobile location data.

“Customs and Border Protection has a long history of impunity and abuse of people's civil and human rights,” says Laura Rivera, an attorney with Just Futures Law, a civil and immigration advocacy legal organization. “Accountability for their wrongdoing has been elusive, and the dynamic involving the abuse of data is simply another aspect of that. As our society adopts more AI, data collection, and surveillance tools, each of us becomes increasingly vulnerable.”

The 2009-2022 dataset shines light on what officers did with the access they already had prior to gaining even more access. According to CBP, digital surveillance tools are supposed to help officers screen travelers and investigate crimes more efficiently. The records, however, reveal how, in case after case, sensitive data collected for law-enforcement purposes was weaponized against private individuals.

Breaches and Queries

At the time these allegations were made, complaints involving CBP personnel were initially routed through the Joint Intake Center, which has since been renamed the CBP Intake Center, and the Joint Intake Case Management System, which CBP and Immigration and Customs Enforcement still use for case tracking. Analysts decided whether each allegation should be retained for information, referred to an employee’s manager, or assigned to the Office of Professional Responsibility investigators as potentially serious misconduct.

Of the almost 300 data-related entries identified by WIRED, 138 were referred to CBP management for review, 78 were serious enough to be assigned to OPR criminal investigators, and 43 were classified as “Information Only,” meaning OPR did not open its own investigation. A smaller number fell into other categories: 12 misconduct allegations were sent for management review, where they were handled internally by the employees’ supervisors rather than by CBP’s central investigators; three were logged as “Law Enforcement Records” cases, meaning criminally investigated misconduct; two were logged as “Immediate Management Actions,” meaning minor misconduct resolved without opening a formal case; and only one as logged as an administrative inquiry, a formal fact-finding investigation conducted by CBP’s Office of Professional Responsibility. CBP withheld 21 cases, citing an exemption protecting active law-enforcement proceedings, suggesting criminal misconduct.

WIRED identified 99 entries involving alleged breaches or unauthorized disclosures of data and 48 explicitly involving improper database queries. Many of these cases happened around 2020, when the pandemic-prompted shift to remote work led CBP employees to start emailing work files to their personal accounts.

Tech.title: There’s a Fatty Liver Epidemic. AI Could Help Get Ahead of It
Tech.content:
All over the world, a slow, insidious change is taking place in the composition of the livers of more than a billion people.

While the presence of fat in a normal, healthy liver is negligible, many adults and even children have livers where fat exceeds 5 percent or even 10 percent of the organ’s total weight. Its unnatural presence causes inflammation, cell damage, and the formation of scar tissue known as fibrosis, all hallmarks of fatty liver disease, a condition that now impacts approximately 30 percent of adults worldwide.

If left to linger, progressive fat accumulation can ultimately lead to liver failure, and it has been linked to an increased risk of cardiovascular disease and various cancers. But the condition typically develops without noticeable symptoms, so it is rarely detected at an early and treatable stage. Even in cases of cirrhosis or advanced scarring of the liver, three-quarters of people are only diagnosed once their condition has become life-threatening.

As a result, growing numbers of specialists are investigating how AI might help. Jeffrey Lazarus, a professor at the CUNY Graduate School of Public Health and Health Policy, suggests that AI tools could be used to comb through vast numbers of electronic health records and pinpoint the people most likely to have accrued worrying amounts of liver fat.

“AI can retrospectively go through massive numbers of hospital visits and lab reports,” says Lazarus. “You can use that to really prioritize who’s at most risk.”

If fatty liver disease can be identified early, much of the damage is highly reversible. In the initial stages, lifestyle changes such as reducing alcohol intake, losing weight through dietary improvements and exercise, and even drinking more coffee have all been shown to be capable of reversing scarring and inflammation. Even for people with moderate to advanced liver scarring, novel treatments such as the GLP-1 medication semaglutide and a drug called resmetirom have been shown to be highly effective therapeutics.

“The liver is a very versatile and interesting organ because it can regenerate, fibrosis can be reversed, and you can be completely healthy again,” says Lazarus. “But traditionally, we’ve focused more on late-stage care and trying to see how long we can keep a patient alive rather than finding them early and preventing the condition from advancing.”

One of the frustrations for Lazarus and others is that while simple, noninvasive means of assessing liver health exist, they are rarely used, even in people known to be at a much higher risk of the consequences of fatty liver disease, such as those with obesity and type 2 diabetes.

The Fib-4 index, for example, rates a person’s risk of advanced liver fibrosis through computing a score of between 0 and 6, based on their age, their levels of two liver enzymes, and their blood-clotting ability. This requires physicians to run a liver blood test, something which is often carried out as part of an annual medical checkup in the US. Doctors also have access to a more accurate, second-line blood test known as the enhanced liver fibrosis test, which measures the levels of two proteins involved in creating scar tissue and an enzyme which inhibits the clearance of scars in the liver.

Using both of these tests in patients with worrying amounts of liver fat has been shown to improve the diagnosis of those with advanced fibrosis by four-fold. But for physicians facing a growing workload and administrative burden, simply adding more testing to the workflow is not felt to be a sustainable option.

“You have to have something that can run in the background or it’s easy to just hit a button and do it,” says Jonathan Dranoff, a professor of medicine at Yale University.

Tech.title: My Favorite Sunrise Alarm Clock Now Tracks Your Sleep — No Wearable Required
Tech.content:
Nasha Addarich Martínez/Jeffrey Hazelwood/CNET

I’ve spent the past few years tracking my sleep. I’ve used smart rings, watches, wristbands and even smart mattress covers. One thing that I learned early on is that most trackers don’t actively improve your sleep. They all give your sleep a score, but most of the time, you don’t even know what the score means or how to improve it.

Hatch is betting that we don’t need to grade our sleep but rather learn which habits can improve it. And ultimately, how rested you feel the next day will be the most important score. The newly released Hatch Sleep Clock, which costs $249, uses what it learns about your sleep to shape your routine for the next night. The clock learns which types of audio help you wind down and what bedtime consistency looks like for you, then it bakes those insights into your night routine.

The most innovative thing about this tracker is that it’s completely contactless. There’s no wearable and no camera. Instead, the clock uses ultra-low-power radio signals to detect breathing and movement from your nightstand. While some may have privacy concerns with any tracking device, Hatch’s reliance on radio signals rather than cameras or microphones offers a significantly more private, passive approach to monitoring.

“We didn’t set out to build another sleep tracker. We set out to help people sleep better,” said Ann Crady Weiss, Co-Founder and CEO of Hatch, in a press release. “For more than a decade, we’ve been learning what helps people build bedtime routines they actually enjoy. Sleep tracking became the missing piece. It helps us understand what works for each person so we can create personalized routines they want to come back to. Rather than simply reporting what happened last night, Hatch Sleep Clock gets you to bed tonight.”

I’ve been using the Hatch Restore 3 for over a year, and I’ve experienced how a good bedtime routine affects your sleep. The Restore 3 nails the experience side, like the lighting, audio library and sensory setup that makes a bedtime routine relaxing. The Sleep Clock takes that experience, learns which sounds help you fall asleep and tailors your bedtime routine to optimize your night.

I love using my Hatch Restore 3 as a gentle sunrise alarm clock and white noise machine. Anna Gragert/CNET

From a sleep science and consumer perspective, this is precisely the gap that exists with most sleep trackers. You can’t fix sleep by letting people know they got poor sleep — they probably feel it in their bodies well before the tracker tells them, anyway. Changes in habits require personalized, timely nudges paired with a routine people want to come back to.

The Sleep Clock breaks down personalization into four areas: listening habits (which audio types actually help you wind down), routine adjustments (tracking bedtime consistency and suggesting when to shift), sleep guidance (cognitive behavioral therapy and good sleep hygiene advice) and feature recommendations (real-time suggestions based on your habits and sleep tracking).

Hatch Plus, which costs $5.99 per month or $59.99 per year, gives you access to the full audio library, which includes over 2,500 sleep-focused tracks, from sleep stories to ASMR to podcasts.

Tech.title: Instagram Has a New Logo for Some Reason
Tech.content:
Instagram has a new logo, and I’m not sure how I feel about it.

The cursive “Instagram” we’ve seen at the top of the app will no longer be entirely cursive, the Meta-owned social media app’s leader says.

“The wordmark at the top of the app hasn’t changed in 10 years, so it was time for a refresh,” Instagram head Adam Mosseri said in the caption of his post unveiling the new logo. Mosseri called the new logo “cleaner and more modern.” It references the original logo’s signature script but is a bit simpler.

Comments under the post were limited and reviews were decidedly mixed. Some Instagram users love it, while others joked about the logo reading “Instagzam,” raising questions about the “r” in the logo. Others questioned the logo change as a whole.

“It’s all been created to flex and grow alongside Instagram and the people who make it a special place,” Instagram said in a blog post.

The company says the new logo will roll out globally throughout the rest of the year and beyond.

Tech.title: Own a KitchenAid Stand Mixer? The Ice Cream Attachment Is a No-Brainer
Tech.content:
Once upon a time, there was a small handful of at-home ice cream makers to choose from. Cuisinart made the best electronic versions — they still rock — while old-timey hand-crank machines offered a retro and muscle-building approach.

Cut to 2026, and there are dozens to choose from, each with a slightly different approach. Ninja’s $250 Creami, a favorite of CNET editors, makes ice cream in 2 minutes, though you’ll need to freeze your custard the night before and find space on the counter to store the machine.

Joey Skladany/CNET KitchenAid Ice Cream Maker Attachment 8.2 $120 at Williams Sonoma $120 at KitchenAid Pros & Cons Fairly inexpensive compared to leading ice cream makers

Very easy to use, clean and store

Yields an authentic soft serve-style ice cream

Takes just 20 to 30 minutes to churn

Allows for customization to create unique flavor profiles Won’t satisfy immediate cravings without a prefrozen bowl

You have to already own a KitchenAid Stand Mixer, which is pricy

Attachment doesn’t easily slide into certain models

Recipe instructions are inconsistent and/or lacking information

Compressor ice cream machines — Cuisinart and Breville both make one — churn ice cream without needing to freeze a mixing bowl or custard, but they’re bulky and expensive.

If you already own a KitchenAid stand mixer, there’s a handy ice cream attachment. At first glance, it makes a ton of sense for those already in possession of the iconic kitchen appliance, best known as the baker’s best friend.

To see if the stand mixer ice cream maker add-on is as simple and sensible as it sounds, I tested it myself. While it has some minor drawbacks compared with standalone machines, its approachable price and slight physical footprint make it a no-brainer for lovers of frozen dessert.

Here’s what I thought of KitchenAid’s $120 ice cream maker attachment.

How KitchenAid’s ice cream attachment works

Here’s how the ice cream maker attachment looked straight out of the box. Joey Skladany/CNET

The KitchenAid ice cream attachment arrives in three pieces: a connecting piece, a churning paddle (also known as a dasher) and an insulated freezer bowl.

To make ice cream at home, you’ll need to freeze the bowl for at least 16 hours before use. Once ready, it replaces any standard metal or wooden bowl on a KitchenAid stand mixer. The dasher is inserted directly into the bowl, while the attachment slides into the metal planetary to connect the machine head to its base (through the top of the dasher).

Your stand mixer transforms into an ice cream maker with this frozen bowl attachment. Joey Skladany/CNET

You should have prepared the ice cream custard in advance and preferably chilled it overnight. Pour it into the bowl and set the appliance to level one (stir mode) to begin churning. Ice cream will be ready in 20 to 30 minutes, depending on the temperature, the thickness of the liquid and the volume. If you have hard mix-ins such as chocolate chips, nuts, or coconut, you can add them halfway through the process.

What I made and how it turned out

Adding eggs to your ice cream base is well worth the extra step. Joey Skladany/CNET

To keep things as simple as possible, I chose to make KitchenAid’s vanilla ice cream recipe. Unfortunately, KitchenAid failed to provide ingredient measurements on its website, but after a bit of digging, I found the correct amounts in the company’s Product Help section.

As a cookbook author with plenty of ice cream-making experience, I doctored the recipe and simmered the following ingredients in a large saucepan over medium-low heat:

The attachment didn’t fit in a Professional 6000 model until I cranked the mixer’s side handle to the point where it met the top part of the dasher, keeping it securely in place. Joey Skladany/CNET

2 cups whole milk

2 cups heavy whipping cream

½ cup maple syrup

2 tsps. vanilla extract

1 tsp. vanilla paste

Pinch of salt

I gently whisked four egg yolks in a small bowl, to which I added a half cup of the warm dairy mixture. Once blended, I poured it into the saucepan and continued mixing with a rubber spatula for 15 minutes, ensuring it never reached a boil.

If you’ve overcooked your egg yolks and your mixture becomes lumpy, pour the liquid through a sieve after removing it from the heat. Otherwise, transfer the liquid to a large bowl, cover with plastic wrap, and refrigerate for at least 3 hours. This is the custard that will be poured into the frozen bowl and used to make vanilla ice cream.

The KitchenAid spun this cold treat in under 30 minutes. Joey Skladany/CNET

What I loved about the KitchenAid ice cream attachment

If you’ve already invested in a KitchenAid stand mixer, which I’d consider to be a kitchen staple, this attachment makes a lot of sense. It’s fairly inexpensive, easy to use, and, perhaps most important, dishwasher-safe (other than the bowl itself). It also yields 2 quarts of ice cream, which is more than enough to feed a small family.

The initial soft serve was delicious and anyone can customize the recipe with flavor and ingredient mix-ins. While I followed KitchenAid’s recipe by heating the ingredients on the stove, this step isn’t necessary. That said, incorporating egg yolks to create a custard will make your ice cream richer and is highly recommended.

The ice cream I churned was as good as anything you’ll find in the freezer aisle. Joey Skladany/CNET

Clean-up was also a breeze — I hand-washed the bowl (after it reached room temperature) and placed the paddle and attachment in the top shelf of my dishwasher.

What I didn’t like about the KitchenAid ice cream attachment

The attachment that is supposed to easily slide into the metal planetary didn’t fit in a Professional 6000 model. Instead, I was forced to crank the mixer’s side handle until it met the top part of the dasher to keep it securely in place.

While the texture was smooth and creamy upon initial churning, I wasn’t a huge fan of its icy texture after it hardened in the freezer for a few hours. This boils down to personal preference, but it’s worth noting for ice cream purists who expect a more velvety mouthfeel.

The insulated bowl also takes up a significant amount of space in a freezer, but it’s a requirement to make ice cream successfully. If it’s not frozen and ready to go, you’ll be unable to satisfy a sudden craving for something sweet and refreshing.

The bottom line

The Ninja Creami earns high marks for its ease and efficiency and is certifiably the industry leader in this space. There are also other ice cream makers that are even more affordable than KitchenAid’s three-part attachment. But if you’re a stand mixer connoisseur and have already splurged on accessories like a dough hook and pasta maker, this addition is a must-have and something to add to your culinary collection.

Make your go-to flavor combinations en masse and enjoy sundaes and splurges all summer long without having to shell out hard-earned cash and leave the comfort of your home. It’s the perfect way to treat yourself — literally — during oppressive heat and long work weeks that demand a bit of caloric indulgence.

Tech.title: Air Fryer Fries Are Good. These Steps Make Them Otherworldly
Tech.content:
French fries have a near-unanimous approval rating, but they’re not so easy to make at home — at least not ones that come out piping hot, crispy and glistening with oil.

Dropping a bag of frozen fries in the air fryer gets them close to that deep-fried taste and crunch, and amen for that. That said, air-fried fries can turn out drier, with a more uneven crisp than those submerged in hot fat. They’re more than edible and far better than oven-baked, but fall just short of perfection.

For fries that taste exactly like the ones at your favorite fast food joint or gastropub, a few easy extra steps are all you need.

7 Best Air Fryers, Out of 20 Tested See at CNET

To amplify your at-home air fryer fries, all you’ll need is a microwave, a bowl of water and some cooking fat. This technique, relayed to me by an air fryer expert, closes the gap between restaurant fries and the so-so versions you’ve been making at home. No boiling oil, no mess, no deep fryer babysitting — just heavenly fries that hit the plate in no more than 15 minutes.

Air fryer fries that taste exactly like deep-fried

Air fryer fries are already an easy snacking win. As I learned from an air fryer expert, they can be way better. Pamela Vachon/CNET

In the age of TikTok, it can be hard to trace the origin of certain hacks, but the method was shared with me by Andreas Hansen, founder and CEO of Fritaire, whose tumbler-based model is especially ideal for this French fry preparation, since it both aids in the texturizing of the exterior of the fries and precludes the need to shake several times during air frying.

The Best Frozen Fries to Cook in an Air Fryer, Tested by CNET See at CNET

A little investigation revealed that Chef Joshua Weissman is frequently credited with bringing attention to the method, but even in his video he gives a shoutout to Chris Young, whose video predates Weissman’s by over a year, and who credits Heston Blumenthal for inspiring the “triple-cooked” method, and so on, and so on.

Regardless of the actual origin of this hack, I’m taking their collective wisdom and applying it to french fries, since the method was specifically developed for thick-cut fries, which, I’m sorry, are steak fries, and not at all the same thing.

What you need for mind-blowing air fryer french fries

Here’s everything you need for the best air fryer fries of your life. Pamela Vachon/CNET

While a majority of what is needed here probably already exists among the various compartments of your kitchen, the supplies you’ll need to gather are:

Frozen french fries (I’m using straight cut, not thick/steak fries)

Large bowl with lid for shaking

Microwave-safe bowl

Microwave

Air fryer

Duck fat, goose fat or beef tallow for best flavor

Salt

Step 1: A quick soak

A quick soak removes excess starch from the frozen potatoes. Pamela Vachon/CNET

Completely counterintuitive to the idea of crunchy fries is the notion that you must first make them soggy, but that is indeed what is recommended.

Straight from the freezer, soak the fries in warm water for 30 seconds to remove some of the starch on their exterior. (30 seconds to 1 minute is recommended for thicker-cut fries.) This is phase one of the “roughing up” process that will eventually create small micro-pockets of additional surface area on the fries, allowing the air fryer to really get a good crisp going.

The goal here is to keep the interior of the fries frozen, so set a timer to prevent over-soaking.

Step 2: Shake vigorously

Yep, now we’re really going to rough up the fries. After draining the soaking water, shake fries vigorously for another 30 seconds or so. The fries should be soft enough just on the exterior to add some texture, but not fall apart entirely. If they do, you’ve soaked too hard in the first step.

The more little craters you can add to the surface of the fries, the more area there is for the air fryer’s air to circulate, giving an unparalleled crisp.

Step 3: Nuke for 5 minutes

Before we go for the big crunch, we’re softening the insides a little. Pamela Vachon/CNET

Before we actually get crunchy, though, things are going to get even softer first. Using a microwave-safe dish with a lid, par-cook the fries for 5 minutes. Since I was using thinner fries, I hedged my bets and went with 50 percent power, but still cooked for the full 5 minutes.

Both Weissman’s and Young’s videos use a plastic container for both soaking and shaking, but we know better than to do that. So long as we’re being extra with this french fry preparation, let’s switch out for a glass or ceramic container, OK?

This par-cooking stage steams the interior of the fries. If you’ve ever found air-fried fries to be hollow, this is the antidote. The unexpected bonus of this step is that microwaving the fries releases a satisfying french-fry aroma.

Unsurprising step: Following the microwave par-cooking, proceed airfrying as normal by placing the fries in a shallow layer in the air fryer and cooking at 400 degrees Fahrenheit for about 12 to 15 minutes (longer for thicker fries), shaking once or twice during the process to ensure all surface areas have access to the circulating air. The goal is golden brown with edges just starting to brown, so that the fries are crispy but still pillowy soft on the inside.

Step 4: Season with cooking fat

Use a drizzle of duck fat to send your fries’ flavor soaring. Pamela Vachon/CNET

While certain items get a little dousing in fat before being cooked in the air fryer, here we’re just using cooking fat as a seasoning, allowing the already-crisped fries to absorb the oil for both texture and flavor.

But not just any fat. For best results — since you’ve gone this far, why not go all the way — look to rendered animal fat such as duck fat, goose fat or beef tallow for a rich flavor boost. Salt to your liking, and voilà: air fryer french fries that are actually kind of fried.

Hungry for more? Learn how to deep-clean your air fryer in three easy steps and see how much less energy it uses than a wall oven.

Tech.title: Equifax Customers Can Claim Part of a $2.2M Class Action Settlement This Month
Tech.content:
Users of Equifax’s consumer credit reports service may be eligible to claim part of an upcoming $2.2 million settlement payout. The case centered on allegations that Equifax violated the Fair Credit Reporting Act, a federal statute that dictates credit reporting companies must “follow reasonable procedures to assure maximum possible accuracy of the information concerning the individual about whom the report relates.”

The class action lawsuit, Bradberry v. Equifax Information Services LLC, alleged that in 2022, Equifax “wrongfully reported duplicates of negative accounts” on certain consumer reports, and that these duplicated debt tradelines are a result of the company having inadequate datakeeping policies and procedures. The lawsuit alleges that Equifax “negligently and recklessly disseminated false and damaging information” regarding the credit of certain customers.

Essentially, the lawsuit alleges that Equifax’s negligent reporting made some customers’ debts appear larger than they actually were, potentially creating situations where affected individuals couldn’t secure loans, credit cards, mortgages and other lines of credit.

The plaintiff, Charmayne Bradberry, filed the suit in the US District Court for the Northern District of Georgia. Bradberry said that she received a report showing the same $305 collection account twice, and that each instance showed separate “opened” and “reported” dates for the debt. She alleges that her credit score dropped severely following this report, which may have prevented her from securing a vital mortgage application.

Bradberry is one of 37,651 customers Equifax identified as having received reports with duplicate debt tradelines.

Equifax has denied any wrongdoing and denied that settlement class members were harmed by its actions, and the court has not ruled in favor of either side. The settlement was agreed upon by both parties, and the court has preliminarily approved the $2.2 million payment, subject to a final approval hearing.

The settlement website is live now. The hearing is scheduled to take place on Oct. 6, during which the court will confirm the settlement sum, allocate funds for attorneys’ fees and create a plan to distribute money to the affected class members.

While some class action lawsuits automatically pay out from the agreed-upon sum, that isn’t the case with Bradberry v. Equifax. Affected individuals need to file a claim and provide valid payment information by Sept. 1 to receive a share of the funds.

If you wish to opt out of or object to the settlement, you must do so by the same Sept. 1 deadline. Failure to do so will mean you remain part of the settlement class and forfeit your right to separately sue Equifax for this incident.

Who can be part of the Equifax settlement?

Not every Equifax customer is automatically eligible to claim part of the settlement. The money is reserved for people who received reports with duplicated collection account information that reflected larger sums of debt than existed in reality.

In order to join, you must meet the following qualifications:

Be a living individual in the US or its territories. Received one of the identified Duplicate Reporting Letters from Equifax between August and September 2022.

The settlement class in this case is extremely well-defined. Equifax identified 37,651 people who received duplicated reports. These individuals are the qualifying settlement class members.

Affected class members need to file a paper claim or log in through the settlement website in order to receive a payout. In order to file a claim online, you need to use the unique settlement member ID number included within the initial communication sent to affected individuals. This communication was sent out via postcard and email.

How much will the Equifax settlement pay out?

The total payment for each claimant is capped at $600, but actual payouts will depend on how many settlement class members file claims and how much money the court sets aside for attorney and administrative fees.

Whether or not settlement class members file a claim, they will receive six months of Equifax Complete credit monitoring services, including credit reports, credit score monitoring and up to $500,000 insurance for identity theft-related expenses.

During the claims process, class members must select a valid payment method for their share of the settlement funds. According to the paper claim form, you can choose to have the money sent to a PayPal, Venmo or Zelle account, a virtual prepaid card or a check.

If you’re eligible to claim a piece of the settlement sum, you must file by Sept. 1. Payments will be distributed after the court’s final approval hearing, assuming there are no appeals.

Tech.title: This $35 Coffee Maker Fits in My Pocket and Comes on All My Camping Trips
Tech.content:
Miir’s Pourigami sets a new standard for portable, pour-over coffee. Nikita Ephanov/CNET

Brewing coffee while camping presents a unique set of challenges. On more occasions than I care to admit, I’ve spilled a freshly made coffee thanks to an unsteady camping table or stone underfoot. But a rigorous day of outdoor adventuring calls for caffeine — full stop. As a professional coffee writer, I demand something more elevated than packets of instant crystals.

Having used several portable brewers, I finally landed on one that ticks the most boxes: The MiiR Pourigami. Once assembled, the pyramid-shaped drip brewer fits atop any travel mug. Taken apart, it’s slim enough to fit into my pants pocket. It functions like standard pour-overs, meaning I can dial in tasting notes to my liking. The laughably simple yet nifty setup lets you play barista in any environment.

Miir Pourigami Coffee Maker $35 at Amazon

The Miir Pourigami brewer in a nutshell

Yup, that’s a coffee maker in my hand. Nikita Ephanov/CNET

Right out of the box, the Pourigami looks sleek. Disassembled, the brewer consists of three thin stainless-steel trapezoids. I can’t imagine the pieces bending or chipping — that’s crucial, as I’m prone to breaking camping equipment. It folds up flat for storage, smaller than 10 by 16 centimeters. Weighing just shy of 8 ounces, the brewer isn’t featherweight, but it offers great portability nevertheless. Contained in an unassuming synthetic case, the Pourigami seamlessly fits into any bag.

I’m terrible at paper origami, but assembling this brewer into the pyramidal shape is a breeze. It only takes me about 20 seconds to slip the three indents into their slots. The completed dripper holds steady without a wobble and comes apart just as easily.

Essential Camping Tech, All Chosen by CNET Editors See at Cnet

Put together, the interior forms a pyramid shape that can accommodate any No. 2 cone-shaped filters. I find that Miir’s own filters, available for purchase online function most reliably, creating steady streams without slipping. The brand’s paper-based filters are compostable, which is a small but satisfying environmental win, but compatible filters are easy to find. Either way, the Miir Pourigami is simple to set up and get to brewing.

Brewing with the Pourigami

The Pourigami functions much like other pour-over coffee devices.

If you’ve used pour-over vessels such as a V60, Chemex or a Kalita Wave, the Miir Pourigami is familiar territory. The dripper requires a hot water source, the aforementioned paper filter, and a cup or carafe to catch the coffee. A kitchen scale and thermometer help brew with utmost accuracy, but I’ve produced solid cups while eyeballing proportions outdoors.

It’s best to follow a brewing ratio to extract the most out of the brewer, especially when familiarizing yourself with its flow. The Miir brand suggests 21 grams for single-origin beans and 23 grams for blends, each extracted with 300 milliliters of water. Using water heated to 90 degrees Celsius, I’ve found these proportions reliable, as long as extraction is completed by the 3.5-minute mark.

The Pourigami functions similarly to a Chemex but with better portability. Taylor Martin/CNET

Compared to my V60, the Miir Pourigami takes longer to drain, so a coarser grind helps keep water moving. As a result, the vessel is best suited for full-bodied cups of medium- and dark-roasted coffees. The grind quality is crucial: You’ll want a coarse yet uniform consistency. I’ve used both the portable MiiR Coffee Hand Grinder and the Baratza Encore to great success; I would avoid using a blade grinder for this setup, though. While I’m away from home, I’ve asked coffee shops to grind beans — I request a consistency one click coarser than a V60. Preground coffee is the most convenient way to brew on the move.

The Pourigami’s steep interior makes saturating coffee grounds easy — no need to carry a gooseneck kettle alongside. I’ve used jet-boil-powered camping kettles and even cooking pots to make excellent cups of coffee, making sure to use hot water that’s off the boil. As long as I’m timing the process, using the Miir Pourigami is undemanding.

What does Pourigami filter coffee taste like?

The coffee I brew turns out light-bodied, but rarely weak or watery. Nikita Ephanov/CNET

As with all pour-over coffee, the beans strongly influence the flavor. I’ve produced the best-tasting MiiR Pourigami cups using medium-roast blends — think grocery-store beans like Stumptown’s Holler Mountain Blend. Such bags respond well to the requisite coarser grind and are forgiving in outdoor scenarios. The Miir Pourigami translates gentle notes of acidity and sweetness, seldom leaning into burnt flavors. The coffee turns out light-bodied, similar to other filter setups, but I’ve never brewed a cup that tastes weak or watery.

If there’s one downside to this dripper, it’s that the coffee occasionally turns out too acidic, a sign of under-extraction. For this reason, I avoid brewing delicate light roasts with the Pourigami — not that I’m packing fancy beans for camping anyway. A bold, balanced medium roast cup hits the spot after a night in a tent.

Is the Pourigami worth it?

Coffee makers don’t get much simpler and more portable than the Pourigami. Nikita Ephanov/CNET

At home, I’m not often assembling my Pourgami, instead settling on the trusty espresso machine or extracting delicate cups of V60. When I’m brewing outside of the house, though, the Pourigami is my top choice. In addition to camping, I’ll pack the brewer away in my suitcase for air travel, making the occasional cup on the go.

Before acquiring a model, I used to camp with a bulky plastic V60 dripper, which I inevitably fractured by cramming it in with the rest of my camping equipment. The AeroPress is sturdier, but it can be difficult to find a surface suitable for firm plunging. Compact and durable, the Miir Pourigami wins on logistical ease, making it easy to incorporate into a car-camping, backpacking or even a bike-packing setup.

Sold for $35, it’s a thoughtfully designed coffee gadget that justifies the price. The inventive design isn’t a trade-off for coffee quality and I’m happy to use the Pourigami several days in a row — the steel material is a breeze to clean. Whether I’m at home or on the move, the brewer doesn’t occupy much space, making it a reliable favorite.

Tech.title: Rivian R1S, R1T See 2027 Updates, Including Second-Row Captain’s Chairs
Tech.content:
American electric vehicle manufacturer Rivian is rolling out 2027 model year updates to the R1S SUV and R1T pickup this week. Alongside a revised trim-level naming scheme that brings the R1 models in line with the newer R2, Rivian’s R1S can now be had with a new second-row captain’s chair configuration that trades a bit of seat capacity for improved comfort and convenience. Meanwhile, the R1T electric truck gets a new all-season wheel-and-tire option, rebalancing on-road range with off-road capability.

Upgraded seating

The biggest material update affects the full-size R1S, which is now available with a six-seat configuration that swaps the SUV’s second-row bench for captain’s chairs. The new buckets get individual armrests that fold flush when not in use and a push-to-release cupholder that accommodates large water bottles, while retaining the bench’s heated surfaces and car-seat tie-downs. The fold-flat design makes way for bulky cargo, but the unobstructed center pass-through allows long, narrow gear like surfboards or skis to stretch through from the rear without having to fold the seats down or give up its six-passenger capacity.

Pricing for the new seat setup ranges from $1,500 to $4,500, depending on the trim level and required and optional equipment.

Rivian says the new second-row configuration is its “most requested interior feature since launch” among R1S shoppers. Brandon De La Cruz / Rivian

Renamed trim levels

Other changes bring Rivian’s flagship trim naming scheme into alignment with the R2. The automaker is largely retiring the Dual, Tri and Quad motor-count naming for most trims. The dual-motor models are now called Premium, offering the same 533 horsepower, 610 pound-feet of torque, and up to 329 miles of range as before. Premium buyers can spec an optional power upgrade that bumps output to 665 hp and 829 lb-ft or upgrade to a bigger battery that stretches the cruising range to 410 miles on the R1S or 420 miles on the R1T.

Performance is the new moniker for the 850-hp tri-motor layout, with 1,103 lb-ft of torque and 371 miles of range. Finally, at the top of the line, the 374-mile Quad trim’s name goes unchanged. It’s still good for 1,025 hp and 1,198 lb-ft, hitting 0 to 60 mph in 2.5 seconds and the quarter-mile in 10.5 seconds in its Launch Mode — a claim I previously verified on a prepped drag strip.

The interior color and material themes for the R1 models have also been renamed to match R2. Premium models are available with Black Mountain (black) or Ocean Coast (gray) upholstery, while Performance and Quad buyers can choose from Slate Sky (gray with walnut wood), Black Mountain Signature (black with ash wood accents) and Ocean Coast Signature (gray with weathered driftwood).

R1T and R1S are now also available in the Silver Esker paint option, a liquid-metal finish first introduced on R2, which replaces LA Silver as the standard no-cost paint option for the 2027 model year.

The larger Rivian R1 models inherit the new Silver Esker paint color from their younger sibling, the R2. Brandon De La Cruz / Rivian

Adventure wheel and tires

R1T gains a new “Adventure” 20-inch all-season wheel-and-tire package as standard equipment on the Premium trim level, trading some on-road range for added off-road traction and grip when compared to some of the larger, lower-friction options available. This combo is also available as a no-cost option on the R1T Performance. That is, unless you count the cost to EPA-estimated range, which drops to 300 miles on the R1T Premium, 380 miles on the Premium Long Range, and 348 miles on the Performance with the new rolling stock.

The 2027 model-year Rivian R1T and R1S are now available to configure on Rivian’s website and in showrooms. R1S starts at $83,990, and R1T starts at $79,990, pricing that is also unchanged from the 2026 model year.

Tech.title: Ninja Just Launched Its First Water Filter. Here’s What It Does That Others Don’t
Tech.content:
Water filtration is a booming category, and at-home units come in a range of formats: under-sink attachments, whole-house systems, water filter pitchers and countertop dispensers.

Ever the innovator, Ninja has jumped into the category with the launch of HydraSense, a slim countertop water filter that removes more than 80 contaminants (including forever chemicals, lead, microplastics and pharmaceuticals) and does a few things its competitors don’t.

The Best Countertop Water Filters, Lab-Tested by CNET See at CNET

I got a firsthand look at the HydraSense at Ninja’s New York headquarters, where the product team walked me through its unique features and also showed off the filter’s pure power by running a batch of Kool-Aid through it.

Here’s what it does.

Filters out the bad stuff but leaves the good

Red Kool-Aid run through the HydraSense came out crystal clear. David Watsky/CNET

Reverse osmosis filters are the best for pure filtering power. The knock is that they strip water of minerals, which can leave water tasting bland. HydraSense’s oversized and especially dense activated carbon filter preserves naturally occurring minerals, including calcium, magnesium and potassium, for better-tasting water.

I sipped some fresh from the spout, and it tasted as crisp and clean as any I’ve had from the many filters I’ve tested.

In a demo, the product team filtered a batch of freshly made red Kool-Aid through the HydraSense. What emerged was perfectly clear liquid that tasted like clean water with no residual fruit punch flavor.

Filters 80+ contaminants, with certifications to prove it

The HydraSense activated carbon filter [left] is bigger and denser than a standard Brita filter.

If you’re wondering how well the filter works, you don’t have to take Ninja’s word for it. The HydraSense is certified by the National Sanitation Foundation, the most rigorous water filter testing body, to remove chlorine, chloramine, lead, volatile organic compounds, PFAS (forever chemicals) and microplastics.

Loads of filters on the market claim to reduce or eliminate these contaminants via in-house or third-party testing, but regulatory certifications leave nothing in question.

Lets you know when the filter needs changing

Many filtration systems require you to guess when the filter needs changing, but not this model. David Watsky/CNET

The bulk of the water filters I’ve tested have no system to let you know when the filter needs changing. It becomes a guessing game, and keeping track of how much water you’ve put through the machine is pretty much impossible.

HydraSense has a built-in monitor that lets you know when the filter is nearing the end of its life so you don’t end up changing it too soon or not soon enough. A single filter is good for 120 gallons, and replacements cost $40.

Filters fast. Like, really fast

When testing countertop water filters for CNET, one downside for most of the machines was slow filtering time — sometimes as much as an hour or more to filter a gallon. The HydraSense uses a unique pressure system to push water through the filter so it dispenses immediately. The feature is especially handy for power hydrators and families that burn through drinking water fast.

I’m a fan of the Rorra gravity filter, but it takes far longer than Ninja’s to strip water of contaminants. David Watsky

While water comes out fast, there’s a handy slow pour setting so you can fill ice trays without making a mess. You can also set the machine to dispense water in pours of 6, 8, 10 and 12 ounces.

Adjustable pour settings allow you to start dispensing and walk away.

The price is right, too

At $200 — currently discounted to $160 for launch — the HydraSense represents one of the best-value water filters I’ve seen. Reverse osmosis systems like the AquaTru Carafe cost nearly twice as much. Gravity filters such as the Rorra and Boroux, which work well but slowly, typically start at around $300 and go up from there.

Ninja’s newly launched HydraSense has a slim build and features you won’t find on most water filters. David Watsky/CNET

It’s closest competitor is the $120 Brita Hub. It too is certified to filter roughly 80 contaminants and does so quickly using a similar pressure system. But there’s no filter life monitor or slow pour settings, and the plastic build is notably cheaper.

The HydraSense is available starting today on Ninja’s website.
